Research programmes — hard cores protected by adjustable auxiliary hypotheses around them.
Anomalous discoveries — surprising results absorbed into existing theory without disruption.
context: Kuhn's 1962 Structure of Scientific Revolutions argued science is not steady accumulation. Normal science works inside a paradigm; revolutions are when the paradigm itself breaks. Lakatos's 'research programmes' is the most serious rival picture.

question: For two thousand years, philosophers said knowledge was justified true belief. In 1963, Gettier published a three-page paper that ended the consensus. What did he show?
answer: You can have a justified true belief that is true only by luck — and luck is not knowledge.
choices: You can have a justified true belief that is true only by luck — and luck is not knowledge.
You can have a justified false belief that becomes knowledge once the world matches it.
You can have a true belief without justification, and call it knowledge by convention.
You can have knowledge that you cannot justify, since some truths exceed reasoned argument.
context: Gettier's 1963 paper offered cases where someone believes something true, has good reason for the belief, yet the reason and the truth come together only by accident. The field has spent sixty years trying to repair the definition. Three pages, lasting fallout.

question: Plato in the Theaetetus offered a clean definition of knowledge that stood for most of philosophy's history. What did he say knowledge was?
answer: A belief that happens to be true and that the believer can back up with good reasons.
choices: A belief that happens to be true and that the believer can back up with good reasons.
A direct seeing of the form, with no need of reasons; the seeing is itself the warrant.
Whatever a community of trained inquirers comes to agree on under steady investigation.
A useful belief that lets the holder act, whether or not the belief strictly maps reality.
context: Plato's tripartite definition — justified, true, belief — survived from the Theaetetus until Gettier's 1963 counterexamples. The other choices map onto rival accounts: Platonic intuition (rival within Plato), Peirce/Dewey-style pragmatism, instrumentalism.

question: Rawls asked you to design society without knowing whether you would be born rich or poor, healthy or sick. He called this the 'veil of ignorance.' What was the point?
answer: Self-interest itself pushes you to choose rules fair to the worst-off, since you may be them.
choices: Self-interest itself pushes you to choose rules fair to the worst-off, since you may be them.
Sympathy for others replaces self-interest, so the chooser picks generous rules from love.
All preferences disappear; pure reason discovers the moral law by itself alone behind the veil.
The chooser maximizes total welfare, since no one knows whose welfare counts as theirs.
context: Rawls's 1971 Theory of Justice ran the thought experiment to fix what fairness meant. The clever move: keep self-interest, just remove the information that lets it tilt. Utilitarianism gives a different answer behind the same veil — which Rawls then attacks.

question: Foot asked you to imagine a runaway trolley headed for five workers. You can pull a lever to divert it onto a side track, where it will kill one. What puzzle did the case open?
answer: Why intentionally killing one feels different from letting the same number die unaided.
choices: Why intentionally killing one feels different from letting the same number die unaided.
Why people prefer certain death of one to the uncertain risk of five they could save.
Why utilitarian arithmetic loses out, in real judgments, to whatever rule the law enforces.
Why bystanders refuse to act even when acting would clearly save more lives than not.
context: Philippa Foot introduced the trolley case in 1967. Her interest was the doctrine of double effect: intended harm versus foreseen-but-unintended harm. The puzzle deepened when Judith Thomson added the footbridge variant, where pushing a man feels worse than pulling the lever.

question: Kripke argued 'water is H2O' is a discovery, not a definition. Once we found out water's chemistry, the identity became necessary — true in every possible situation. What followed?
answer: Some necessary truths can only be discovered by experiment, not by armchair analysis.
choices: Some necessary truths can only be discovered by experiment, not by armchair analysis.
All necessary truths are analytic, since necessity belongs only to relations among ideas.
Identity statements like 'water is H2O' are contingent — water could have had other chemistry.
Empirical inquiry can never reach necessity; chemistry tells us what is, never what must be.
context: Kripke's Naming and Necessity (1972) broke the long-standing tie between 'necessary' and 'knowable a priori.' Water might have looked different — but whatever it actually is, it could not have been anything else. Hume held the position offered in the second distractor.

question: Lewis took 'possible worlds' talk literally. When we say it was possible Napoleon won at Waterloo, he said, we mean there is a real world where he did. What did he call this view?
answer: Modal realism — every way the world could have been is a complete world that genuinely exists.
choices: Modal realism — every way the world could have been is a complete world that genuinely exists.
Modal fictionalism — possible-world talk is useful pretense; no such worlds are really out there.
Conceptualism — possibilities are mental constructions, real only insofar as some mind holds them.
Linguistic conventionalism — what counts as 'possible' is whatever community usage permits.
context: Lewis's On the Plurality of Worlds (1986) defended modal realism not as metaphor but as the simplest theory of what 'possible' really means. Most philosophers think the price is too high. The distractors are the live rivals — fictionalist, conceptualist, conventionalist accounts.

question: Someone says: 'this sentence is false.' If it is true, then it is false. If it is false, then it is true. What is this puzzle?
answer: The liar paradox — a sentence that can be neither consistently true nor consistently false.
choices: The liar paradox — a sentence that can be neither consistently true nor consistently false.
The sorites paradox — small unnoticed changes adding up to a clearly different situation.
Russell's paradox — a set containing exactly the sets that are not members of themselves.
Zeno's dichotomy — any motion must first cover half a distance, then half the rest forever.
context: Attributed to Epimenides in antiquity, the liar paradox forced 20th-century logic to rethink truth. Tarski concluded that a language cannot consistently contain its own truth-predicate. The distractors are three other famous paradoxes the player may have heard named together.

question: Zeno asked you to imagine an arrow in flight. At any instant, it occupies its own length exactly. At that instant, it is not moving. What did he conclude?
answer: Each instant is a snapshot of rest, and a sum of rests is still rest — unmoving frames can never add up to motion.
choices: Each instant is a snapshot of rest, and a sum of rests is still rest — unmoving frames can never add up to motion.
Motion is real, but cannot be made of instants — time must be a single unbroken whole, not a series of frames.
Motion is real and made of instants; at each one the arrow has a definite speed, and those speeds add up.
Motion exists only relative to an observer; without one, the arrow neither moves nor stays still at all.
context: Zeno's arrow paradox defended Parmenides: appearance shows change, but reason proves change incoherent. The puzzle: an instant has zero duration, and within zero duration nothing moves — so motion must somehow be assembled from non-motion, which Zeno took to be impossible. The calculus eventually modeled instantaneous velocity as a limit, dissolving the paradox at a mathematical level. Each distractor is a real philosophical reply — Bergsonian continuity, the modern calculus answer, relationalism.

question: Nagel imagined a bat — flying in the dark, navigating by bouncing echoes off insects. Even with perfect knowledge of bat biology, he said, you would miss something. What?
answer: What it is actually like, from the inside, to be a bat using echolocation to find its way.
choices: What it is actually like, from the inside, to be a bat using echolocation to find its way.
How the bat learned to echolocate, and whether its first attempts at flight ever succeeded.
What ordinary bats would say about being a bat, if only they were taught to use language.
Whether the bat's brain is conscious in any way at all, given how small the brain really is.
context: Nagel's 1974 paper 'What is it like to be a bat?' argued there is a subjective character to experience that objective description leaves out. Echolocation is alien enough that even imagining your way in stalls. Whether bats are conscious (a distractor) is a different question.

question: Chalmers drew a line between the 'easy problems' of consciousness and the 'hard problem.' The easy ones include attention, memory, behavior. What made the hard one hard?
answer: Explaining why any physical process is accompanied by inner experience at all, rather than darkness.
choices: Explaining why any physical process is accompanied by inner experience at all, rather than darkness.
Explaining how neurons firing in patterns produce the rapid behaviors observed in living animals.
Explaining why some animals have consciousness while others with similar brain sizes do not.
Explaining how the brain stores memories long enough for an animal to recognize its own kin.
context: Chalmers's 1995 essay drew the easy/hard distinction. The easy ones may be unsolved but admit familiar scientific treatment. The hard one asks why there is something it is like to be a brain — a question the easy ones never reach. The distractors are real easy-problem questions.

question: Anselm in 1078 offered an argument for God using only the meaning of a word. God, he said, is 'that than which nothing greater can be conceived.' What was his move?
answer: A being that exists in reality is greater than one in thought; so the greatest must exist.
choices: A being that exists in reality is greater than one in thought; so the greatest must exist.
A being so widely worshipped across cultures must reflect a shared object behind the practice.
A being whose works show design and order proves a designer behind the designed world.
A being able to inspire belief at all must have caused that belief by acting on the mind.
context: Anselm's 'ontological argument' in the Proslogion tries to derive God's existence from the concept of God alone. Aquinas rejected it; Descartes revived it; Kant attacked it; Plantinga reformulated it. The distractors are the other classical arguments — consensus, design, and a religious-experience variant.

question: Pascal said you must bet whether God exists — living is itself a wager. If you bet yes and you are right, you win infinity; wrong, you lose almost nothing. What did he conclude?
answer: Wager yes — when the stakes are infinite, even a small probability swamps any finite cost.
choices: Wager yes — when the stakes are infinite, even a small probability swamps any finite cost.
Wager no — only honest unbelief, not calculated belief, could be of value to a truthful God.
Refuse the wager — rational belief must follow evidence, never the size of imagined payoffs.
Take your community's bet — religious truth is a social inheritance, not a personal choice.
context: Pascal's wager appears in the Pensées (published 1670, after his death). He thought reason could not settle God's existence directly, but could rank the bets. Critics from William James to modern decision theorists have probed the wager — including its 'many gods' problem.

question: Kant said calling a sunset beautiful is odd. You are not just reporting your private pleasure — you claim, somehow, that others ought to agree. What did he find strange about this?
answer: Beauty judgments demand universal agreement without resting on a rule that could compel it.
choices: Beauty judgments demand universal agreement without resting on a rule that could compel it.
Beauty judgments are pure taste, like preferring strawberries — disagreement is meaningless.
Beauty judgments are moral judgments in disguise — sunsets are beautiful because they are good.
Beauty judgments depend on training, so only the educated few are entitled to make them.
context: Kant's 1790 Critique of Judgment called this the antinomy of taste. We treat 'this is beautiful' as objective enough to argue about, yet we cannot produce the rule that would settle the argument. Hume's relativism, a moralist reading, and aristocratic taste are the distractors.

question: Burke and Kant noticed that standing at the edge of an Alpine cliff produces a feeling unlike ordinary beauty. The view is too vast, almost frightening — yet you cannot look away. What did they call it?
answer: The sublime — pleasure at confronting what overwhelms the senses but not the mind.
choices: The sublime — pleasure at confronting what overwhelms the senses but not the mind.
The picturesque — a beauty depending on variety, roughness, and irregular texture.
The grotesque — beauty mixed with the unsettling, like gargoyles seen up close.
The numinous — the felt presence of the holy, both fascinating and full of dread.
context: Burke (1757) and Kant (1790) gave the sublime its modern form. The sense of being small before something vast — storms, mountains, the starry sky — became central to Romantic art. The distractors are real adjacent categories from Gilpin, Ruskin, and Rudolf Otto.

question: Singer asked you to imagine walking past a shallow pond where a child is drowning. Saving her would ruin your expensive shoes — nothing worse. Almost everyone would wade in. What did he conclude?
answer: If proximity does not change duty, distant strangers in like need have an equal claim on us.
choices: If proximity does not change duty, distant strangers in like need have an equal claim on us.
Special obligations to our own children make moral concern for strangers always secondary.
Charity is praiseworthy but never required — it lies beyond the line of basic moral duty.
Moral feelings track an evolved tribe; philosophy should accept that limit, not stretch it.
context: Singer's 1972 'Famine, Affluence, and Morality' argued the distance between you and the drowning child is morally irrelevant. The pond logic, extended, demands radical giving. Distractors are real rivals — partialism (Williams), supererogation, evolutionary morality.

question: Leopold once shot a wolf and watched the 'fierce green fire' die in its eyes. The county killed the wolves; deer multiplied; the mountains were stripped bare. He called the lesson 'thinking like a mountain.' What did he mean?
answer: A piece of land has a long-term welfare that the eye, focused on immediate gain, misses.
choices: A piece of land has a long-term welfare that the eye, focused on immediate gain, misses.
Nature is a hierarchy with predators on top; removing one collapses the rank order beneath.
Wilderness has rights of its own that override any human claim to use or improve the land.
Ecology is a science, and political decisions about land belong to the trained ecologist.
context: Leopold's 1949 Sand County Almanac founded modern conservation ethics. The wolf-deer-mountain chain is its central image. Distractors are real rival positions: trophic-cascade ecology without ethics, deep-ecology rights talk, technocratic land management.

question: Turing in 1950 proposed a game. A judge types to a hidden human and a hidden machine. If the judge cannot tell which is which, the machine passes. What did he claim this settled?
answer: Whether to call something a thinker is a question about behavior, not inner mechanism.
choices: Whether to call something a thinker is a question about behavior, not inner mechanism.
Whether a machine truly understands — indistinguishable replies must rest on understanding.
Whether a machine is conscious — fluent conversation could only come from inner experience.
Whether a machine has a soul — any being that could fool a careful judge must possess one.
context: Turing's 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence' (1950) deliberately replaced the metaphysical question with an operational one. Critics — Searle most famously — argue passing the test would not settle understanding, consciousness, or anything else. The distractors are exactly those inflations.

question: Pinker in The Blank Slate (2002) argued against the view that had dominated 20th-century social science: that the mind is born empty, shaped only by environment. What did he claim instead?
answer: The mind comes with structure built by evolution; culture writes onto a slate not really blank.
choices: The mind comes with structure built by evolution; culture writes onto a slate not really blank.
The mind comes from a soul implanted at conception; biology shapes the body, not what is thought.
The mind reflects whichever class the person is born into; material conditions explain the rest.
The mind has no real structure at all — what we call human nature is a name for habit alone.
context: Pinker named the dominant view 'the Blank Slate' (Locke), with 'the Noble Savage' (Rousseau) and 'the Ghost in the Machine' (Descartes) as its companions. The distractors map onto the second and third of those, plus a Marxist-environmentalist variant.

question: Sowell in A Conflict of Visions argued most political fights trace to a deeper disagreement about humans themselves. He named two visions. What was the split?
answer: Whether human nature is fixed (so policy is tradeoffs) or improvable (so policy solves problems).
choices: Whether human nature is fixed (so policy is tradeoffs) or improvable (so policy solves problems).
Whether the individual is wiser than the group, or the group wiser than any individual in it.
Whether the rich are entitled to their gains, or the poor to a share of the rich's surplus.
Whether reason or revelation should settle disputes about how a society ought to be ordered.
context: Sowell's 1987 book named the 'constrained' vision (Burke, Smith, the Founders) and the 'unconstrained' vision (Godwin, Condorcet). For one, every policy choice is a painful tradeoff; for the other, settling for less than the best is failure. The other splits are real, just not Sowell's.

question: Hayek wrote The Road to Serfdom in 1944, while the war against Nazi Germany was still being fought. He warned the West that even well-meaning planning carried a danger. What was the core warning?
answer: Centralized economic control concentrates power, and concentrated power crowds out freedom.
choices: Centralized economic control concentrates power, and concentrated power crowds out freedom.
Socialist parties begin honestly, but their leaders, once in office, betray the workers below.
Postwar Europe lacked maturity for self-government; only constitutional monarchy kept it free.
Communism and fascism share a doctrine of racial destiny that liberal democracies must reject.
context: Hayek's book argued the danger was structural, not personal — well-intentioned planners would find themselves needing more power to make their plans work. The distractors are real adjacent positions: rotten-leadership thesis, monarchist conservatism, and a totalitarianism conflation Hayek rejected.

question: Bastiat in 1850 told of a careless boy who breaks a shopkeeper's window. Neighbors said: good news — it gives the glazier work. Bastiat said they were missing something. What?
answer: The shoes, the book, the dinner the shopkeeper would have spent the money on instead.
choices: The shoes, the book, the dinner the shopkeeper would have spent the money on instead.
The damage to the boy's character; petty vandalism in childhood ripens into worse crimes later.
The trust between neighbors, eroded whenever one refuses to pay for what he himself broke.
The role of insurance, which alone makes such accidents bearable without burdening third parties.
context: Bastiat's 'broken window fallacy' shows any visible gain has invisible costs — what would have been done with the same resource. Distractors are real adjacent readings (moral, communitarian, institutional), none of which is Bastiat's economic point. The lesson opens opportunity cost as a moral category.

question: Solzhenitsyn wrote The Gulag Archipelago in secret, hiding chapters with different friends, never keeping the whole manuscript in one place. Discovery would have cost his life. What did the book prove to the West?
answer: The Soviet camp system was built into the regime from 1918, not a deformation of Stalin alone.
choices: The Soviet camp system was built into the regime from 1918, not a deformation of Stalin alone.
A literary tradition could outlast any tyranny, since words on paper outlive every police force.
America's Cold War rhetoric was largely accurate, even if its proxy wars were often badly chosen.
Socialism in principle was sound; only Russian backwardness had produced the camps in this case.
context: Solzhenitsyn's three-volume work, smuggled west and published in 1973, dated the camps to a Lenin decree of 1918. The 'Stalin aberration' line popular with Western fellow-travelers could not survive the documentation. The distractors are real adjacent readings the book was meant to defeat.

question: Havel described a Prague greengrocer who hangs in his window the sign Workers of the World, Unite. He does not believe it. The customers know he does not. Havel asked what the sign really says. What is his answer?
answer: It says: I know what I am supposed to do, and I am doing it — please leave me alone.
choices: It says: I know what I am supposed to do, and I am doing it — please leave me alone.
It says the regime is failing; only failing regimes need slogans in every window pane.
It says workers should unite; the man agrees, even if his customers are uncertain too.
It says nothing at all; shop-window slogans are background noise the neighborhood ignores.
context: Havel's 1978 essay The Power of the Powerless called this post-totalitarianism — a regime sustained not by terror but by the ritual self-implication of citizens in a story none of them believes. The distractors include the regime's reading, a sincere reading, and a denial that signs do anything.

question: King in 1963 dreamed of a day when his children would be judged 'not by the color of their skin but by the content of their character.' What older argument was he extending?
answer: The founders' natural-rights claim — Declaration promises must apply to every American.
choices: The founders' natural-rights claim — Declaration promises must apply to every American.
The Marxist class-struggle claim — legal equality is hollow until economics is transformed.
The black-nationalist claim — the rights of black Americans must come from a separate polity.
The progressive social-engineering claim — government must reshape attitudes through policy.
context: King grounded the speech in the American founding documents and the prophets — Lincoln, Jefferson, Isaiah, Amos. The distractors are three real rival traditions of mid-20th-century black political thought (CPUSA-aligned Marxism, Garveyite nationalism, technocratic progressivism), each of which King knew and rejected.

question: Lincoln at Gettysburg in 1863 gave a two-minute speech that listed no battles. He tied the war to a date almost a century older. What text was the war about?
answer: The Declaration of Independence — its claim that all men are created equal had to come true.
choices: The Declaration of Independence — its claim that all men are created equal had to come true.
The Constitution of 1787 — the federal Union must be preserved against any state's secession.
The Northwest Ordinance — new western territories must always enter the Union as free states.
The Mayflower Compact — the Puritan ideal of self-governing community bound by covenant.
context: Lincoln's address opened 'Four score and seven years ago' — back to 1776, not 1787. He read the war as the test of whether a nation founded on the Declaration's promise could endure. The distractors are real founding texts Lincoln could have invoked, but did not — and the difference is the point.

question: Madison, Hamilton, and Jay wrote 85 essays under the name 'Publius' in 1787, urging New Yorkers to ratify the new Constitution. What was the collection arguing for?
answer: That a single extended republic could govern free people better than a loose league of small states.
choices: That a single extended republic could govern free people better than a loose league of small states.
That Britain's unwritten constitution should be the model for a written American one to come.
That elected presidents — not hereditary executives — would protect the rights of the citizen.
That a national bank should be chartered to manage the new federal government's growing debt.
context: The Federalist defended the proposed Constitution against the Anti-Federalists, who feared a strong central government would swallow the states. Madison's Federalist 10 made the famous argument that a large republic, not a small one, best controls faction. The distractors are real period debates.

question: Simone de Beauvoir opened The Second Sex in 1949 with a sentence that became famous: 'One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman.' What was she pressing?
answer: What it means to be a woman is shaped by social formation, not fixed by biological birth.
choices: What it means to be a woman is shaped by social formation, not fixed by biological birth.
Biological sex itself is a social construction with no underlying biological reality at all.
Adult identity, once formed by experience, can never afterward be revised by new evidence.
Women and men reason in fundamentally different modes no shared education could bridge.
context: Beauvoir's existentialist feminism distinguished sex (the biological fact) from gender (the formed role). She kept the distinction precise. The first distractor pushes her line past where she drew it; the others are real rival positions in 20th-century thought that she explicitly rejected.

question: Across many Southern African languages runs the saying: 'a person is a person through other persons.' Tutu and Ramose called it Ubuntu and read it as a philosophical claim. What is the claim?
answer: A self comes into being through recognition by, and bond to, a surrounding community of persons.
choices: A self comes into being through recognition by, and bond to, a surrounding community of persons.
Each person holds inalienable rights from birth; community is a contract that adds nothing real.
The self is illusion; liberation is dissolving the ego into an impersonal cosmic order beyond ties.
Moral worth lies in autonomous rational willing; others matter only because reason commands respect.
context: Ubuntu, developed philosophically by Desmond Tutu and Mogobe Ramose among others, frames personhood relationally rather than individually. The distractors map onto Locke's individualist rights, Advaita Vedanta's dissolution of self, and Kant's autonomy — three real rival accounts of what makes a self.

question: Vine Deloria Jr. titled his 1973 book God Is Red and argued Western and tribal religions answer different opening questions. What did he say the difference was?
answer: Western religion organizes meaning around time and events; tribal religion around place and land.
choices: Western religion organizes meaning around time and events; tribal religion around place and land.
All religions express the same perennial truths in different wrappers; the wrappers vary, not the core.
Religion is the alienated form of social production; both Western and tribal religions cloak relations.
Genuine religion arises only from private mystical experience; ritual and community are later add-ons.
context: Deloria, a Standing Rock Sioux scholar, contrasted sacred time (Sinai, Easter) with sacred place (Bear Butte, Blue Lake). The distractors map onto Huxley's perennialism, Marx's religion-as-alienation, and James's experiential individualism — three real rival framings of what religion is.

question: Stoics and Buddhists, separated by centuries and continents, both diagnosed human suffering as rooted in a wrong relation with desire. Where did they agree on the root cause?
answer: Both blamed attachment to fleeting goods — clinging to what cannot last produces the suffering.
choices: Both blamed attachment to fleeting goods — clinging to what cannot last produces the suffering.
Both denied desire any role at all — the sage simply ceases to want, and cessation is wisdom.
Both treated suffering as illusion — the awakened person sees the pain as empty and unreal.
Both prescribed withdrawal from public life — only the monk or hermit attains the inward peace.
context: Epictetus held suffering comes from judgments about events, not events themselves. The Buddha named tanha — craving — as the second noble truth. They differ on technique: Stoics retrain judgment; Buddhists follow the eightfold path. The distractors are caricatures both schools would reject.

question: A politician's tax plan is criticized only by noting he once cheated on his own taxes. The plan itself goes unaddressed. This move has a Latin name. What is it?
answer: Ad hominem — attacking the arguer rather than the argument they made.
choices: Ad hominem — attacking the arguer rather than the argument they made.
Tu quoque — replying that you also fail rather than answering the point.
Red herring — dragging in something unrelated to distract from the issue.
Straw man — attacking a weakened version of the opponent's real claim.
context: Ad hominem attacks the person, not the argument. A flawed person can still be right; a saint can still be wrong. The argument's truth is independent of who makes it.

question: Someone says trade should be expanded gradually. Their opponent shouts back: 'so you want to ship every job overseas.' The opponent has replaced the real claim with a wilder one. What is this move?
answer: Straw man — attacking a distorted version of the opponent's claim.
choices: Straw man — attacking a distorted version of the opponent's claim.
Red herring — pulling discussion onto a different unrelated topic.
Slippery slope — claiming one step must lead to a disastrous result.
Loaded question — asking something that presupposes a disputed point.
context: A straw man is easier to knock down because you built it. The fix is the steel man: state the opponent's view in its strongest form, then engage that.

question: Aristotle laid out a three-line form: 'All men are mortal. Socrates is a man. So Socrates is mortal.' The conclusion is forced by the form alone. What did he call this?
answer: Syllogism — two premises and a conclusion forced by the form.
choices: Syllogism — two premises and a conclusion forced by the form.
Enthymeme — an argument with one premise left unstated.
Sorites — a chain of premises sliding toward a conclusion.
Dialectic — testing rival claims through question and answer.
context: The syllogism is the foundation of Western formal logic. The reasoning works because of its structure — no matter what fills the slots, the conclusion is locked in.

question: Socrates fought in three campaigns and once saved Alcibiades in battle. At his trial he insisted philosophy itself was military service. What had he been doing?
answer: Acting as a gadfly stinging a noble horse — keeping Athens awake to its confusions.
choices: Acting as a gadfly stinging a noble horse — keeping Athens awake to its confusions.
Serving as physician of the soul — diagnosing the city's moral sicknesses like Hippocrates.
Working as midwife of ideas — helping citizens deliver truths he himself did not possess.
Standing watchman at the gates — guarding against new gods that would corrupt the virtues.
context: The gadfly image is in the Apology. The horse — Athens — is too big and lazy without its gadfly. The metaphor takes weight knowing Athens killed its gadfly.

question: Plato founded a school outside Athens around 387 BC, on land that had been a grove sacred to a local hero. The grove gave the school its name — now used for every learning institution. What was it?
answer: The Academy — its inscription warned the geometrically untrained not to enter.
choices: The Academy — its inscription warned the geometrically untrained not to enter.
The Lyceum — Aristotle's rival walking-school in the grove of Apollo Lyceus.
The Garden — Epicurus's community, men and women and slaves studying together.
The Stoa — the Painted Porch where Zeno's school took the name Stoicism.
context: Plato's Academy ran in various forms for nearly 900 years before Justinian closed it in 529 AD. Aristotle studied there for twenty years before founding his own rival school nearby.

question: Aristotle was tutor to a 13-year-old prince at the Macedonian court for three years. The boy would later conquer the known world from Greece to the Punjab. Who was the student?
answer: Alexander the Great — who carried Greek language and philosophy from Persia to India.
choices: Alexander the Great — who carried Greek language and philosophy from Persia to India.
Pyrrho of Elis — the skeptic who marched with Alexander and met the Indian sages.
Antisthenes the Cynic — older student of Socrates and ancestor of the Cynic tradition.
Speusippus the Academic — Plato's nephew who took over the Academy after his uncle.
context: Alexander reportedly slept with a copy of the Iliad annotated by Aristotle under his pillow. The young king sent biological specimens back from his campaigns for his old teacher's research.

question: Epictetus had been born a slave in Rome and lived with a permanent limp from his master's cruelty. After manumission, he taught Stoic philosophy in Greece. What did he say his philosophy was for?
answer: Sorting what is in our power from what is not — wanting only what is in our power.
choices: Sorting what is in our power from what is not — wanting only what is in our power.
Rising above attachments of family, city, and reputation — each binds the soul to fortune.
Cultivating the soul's natural impulse toward pleasure — nature shows us what is good.
Sharpening the mind by suspending judgement — tranquility replaces the restless arguing.
context: Epictetus's whole philosophy comes from the moment-by-moment practice of his sorting rule: this — is it up to me, or not? The slave's limp had taught him the rule on his body.

question: Zeno of Citium had been a Phoenician merchant whose ship sank off Greece around 300 BC. Stranded in Athens, he read a book on Socrates and became a philosopher. He founded a school named for where it met. What was it?
answer: The Stoa — the Painted Porch in Athens, source of the name Stoicism.
choices: The Stoa — the Painted Porch in Athens, source of the name Stoicism.
The Garden — Epicurus's suburban plot for cultivating untroubled calm.
The Lyceum — Aristotle's grove of Apollo where students walked while learning.
The Cynics' Tub — Diogenes' wine-jar dwelling in the Athenian marketplace.
context: Zeno's biography became part of his philosophy: a shipwreck turned out to be the best business decision he ever made. Loss had revealed what was actually his — his judgements, and nothing else.

question: Descartes was a French soldier on campaign in the winter of 1619 when, snowed into a small heated room, he had three vivid dreams in one night. He took them as a sign. What project did he set himself?
answer: To rebuild all knowledge from the ground up — discarding every belief he could doubt.
choices: To rebuild all knowledge from the ground up — discarding every belief he could doubt.
To devote himself to Galileo's new mechanical natural philosophy of motion.
To return to the Catholic faith of his upbringing and become a Jesuit priest.
To found a new philosophical school in Paris against the scholastic teachers.
context: Descartes saw the dreams as divine confirmation of his vocation. He vowed a pilgrimage to Loreto and spent the next twenty years building the Meditations — Western philosophy's most influential rebuild from the ground up.

question: Anaxagoras was a wealthy Athenian who walked away from his estates to do philosophy. Asked why he didn't care for his fatherland, he pointed at the sky and said his fatherland was up there. What did he say set the cosmos in order?
answer: Nous — Mind — which stood apart from material things and started the first rotation.
choices: Nous — Mind — which stood apart from material things and started the first rotation.
Logos — Reason — which permeated material things and unified their changes into one process.
Apeiron — the Boundless — which lay behind visible elements and emitted them through separation.
Eros — Love — which drew opposed elements together, balanced by an opposite force of strife.
context: Anaxagoras's Nous influenced Socrates briefly (Plato has Socrates report his disappointment in the Phaedo) — but Socrates wished Anaxagoras had used Nous to explain WHY things are good, not just as a mechanical starter. The dissatisfaction sparked Platonic teleology.

question: Heraclitus called fire the basic stuff of the world, but he meant something stranger than burning logs. What did he say fire was a figure for?
answer: The endless transformation that is reality itself — one unified process behind every visible change.
choices: The endless transformation that is reality itself — one unified process behind every visible change.
An eternal substance that, unlike water or air, can never itself be transformed or destroyed.
The divine spark hidden inside each soul that returns to its source when the body dies.
A physical element more refined than air, condensing downward into all other forms of matter.
context: For Heraclitus, fire is reality's master metaphor: it is never the same flame twice, yet it remains itself. The world burns continuously — what we call 'things' are just the shapes the burning takes for a moment.

question: Heraclitus said the road up the mountain and the road down it are one and the same road. What philosophical claim was this image meant to support?
answer: Opposites are two aspects of one thing, and the tension between them is what holds the world together.
choices: Opposites are two aspects of one thing, and the tension between them is what holds the world together.
Every path eventually returns the traveler to where they began, since space curves back on itself.
Words like 'up' and 'down' are mere convention; the world itself contains no real directions at all.
Motion is impossible — what looks like a journey is only a string of unconnected stationary moments.
context: Heraclitus called this the 'unity of opposites.' Hot and cold, sleeping and waking, life and death — each pair names one continuous process. Strip away the tension and you would not get peace; you would get nothing at all.

question: Parmenides argued that 'nothing' cannot exist, because the moment you speak of it you have made it into a something. What strange conclusion did he then draw?
answer: Change cannot be real, since change would require a thing to pass into what-is-not, and what-is-not cannot be.
choices: Change cannot be real, since change would require a thing to pass into what-is-not, and what-is-not cannot be.
Matter is made of tiny indivisible particles, and their rearrangement only appears to us as change.
All things are fire transforming endlessly; what looks like stasis is just slow, invisible burning.
Time is something the mind lays over a world that in itself stands wholly outside any sequence.
context: Parmenides bequeathed Western philosophy its first proof — and a baffling one. If 'is not' is unsayable, then nothing can come into being or pass away. The river we see flowing must, behind appearance, be a single unchanging block.

question: Zeno of Elea imagined an arrow in flight. At any single instant, the arrow is not moving — it occupies a space equal to its own length. What was Zeno trying to prove?
answer: If motion is made of motionless instants, then motion itself is impossible — defending Parmenides on change.
choices: If motion is made of motionless instants, then motion itself is impossible — defending Parmenides on change.
Any physical object can be cut in half without limit, so matter has no smallest indivisible building block.
The arrow's path must be determined in advance, so human freedom is an illusion in a fated universe.
Sense-perception fails for fast objects, so we should not trust the eyes about anything in motion at all.
context: Zeno was Parmenides' student, and his paradoxes were arguments by reductio: if you accept that motion is real, you end up with contradictions. The arrow paradox would wait for calculus, 2,200 years later, to be properly dissolved.

question: Pythagoras heard hammers of different weights strike a forge and noticed the sounds formed harmonies. From this he built a sweeping claim about reality itself. What did he conclude?
answer: The deepest structure of reality is mathematical — numbers and ratios, not water or fire, are what things are.
choices: The deepest structure of reality is mathematical — numbers and ratios, not water or fire, are what things are.
The natural world is alive throughout, and even stones carry a faint share of the same soul we have.
Music has a moral effect on the listener, so cities should regulate which scales their citizens hear.
Craft skill arises only by long imitation, so the smith and the philosopher learn in the same way.
context: The hammer story is likely legend, but the insight was real: pluck a string at half its length and you get the octave; at two-thirds, the fifth. Pythagoras took this as proof that whole-number ratios run beneath everything — even the planets, he thought, made music.

question: Pythagoras forbade his followers from eating beans and ordered five years of silence before they could speak in his school. These rules pointed toward what core doctrine?
answer: Souls move from body to body after death, so the body must be purified to ready the soul for its journey.
choices: Souls move from body to body after death, so the body must be purified to ready the soul for its journey.
Knowledge is recovered only by careful logical proof, so disciples must master geometry before speaking.
The gods envy mortal speech, so silence and abstinence are needed to avoid drawing their dangerous notice.
All living beings share one single soul, so eating any plant or animal does harm to the eater's own self.
context: Pythagoras taught metempsychosis — the soul moves from body to body, possibly across species. Diet and silence were spiritual training. He once reportedly stopped a man beating a dog, claiming to recognize the voice of a dead friend in its yelps.

question: Xenophanes mocked his contemporaries for picturing gods in their own image — Greeks made Greek-looking gods, Thracians red-haired ones. What larger point was he driving at?
answer: That human ideas of the divine reflect the humans more than the divine, and so must be sharply distrusted.
choices: That human ideas of the divine reflect the humans more than the divine, and so must be sharply distrusted.
That the gods of different peoples are real but local, each one ruling only the land where it is worshipped.
That the gods do not exist at all, and stories of them are tools used by rulers to control their subjects.
That the gods, while real, lack any moral character and care nothing about how humans choose to act.
context: Xenophanes drove the point home with a joke: if horses and oxen had hands, he said, they would draw their gods as horses and oxen. He was not quite an atheist — he believed in one supreme deity, unlike anything human — but he was the first systematic critic of religious projection.

question: Empedocles claimed he was a god and jumped into Mount Etna to prove it — legend says only a bronze sandal was found at the rim. His cosmology was equally bold: four elements driven by two cosmic forces with surprising names. What were they?
answer: Love and Strife — one binding the elements into stable things, the other tearing them apart.
choices: Love and Strife — one binding the elements into stable things, the other tearing them apart.
Light and Darkness — one revealing the elements in their true forms, the other hiding them.
Reason and Necessity — one ordering the elements toward purpose, the other toward decay.
Number and Motion — one fixing the elements in stable ratios, the other carrying change.
context: Empedocles' cycle is a kind of cosmic breathing: Love draws the four elements together into rocks, plants, animals; Strife pulls them back apart. Neither wins for long. He claimed he had himself lived as a bush, a bird, a fish — and the Etna leap was meant to prove his divinity to skeptics.

question: Bastiat in 1845 wrote a mock petition from candle-makers begging parliament to block out the sun, whose free light undercut their trade. What was the joke's target?
answer: Any protectionist case that treats a cheaper source of supply as an injury rather than a gain to consumers.
choices: Any protectionist case that treats a cheaper source of supply as an injury rather than a gain to consumers.
Any subsidy from the state to a producer who has not first proven the social usefulness of the trade.
Any law against a private monopoly when the same privilege is freely granted to a politically favored guild.
Any tax on imports that fails to fall in proportion to the buyer's wealth rather than the good's price.
context: The candle-makers complained of a rival who 'floods our market with light at a price ridiculously low.' By demanding parliament shutter every window, Bastiat showed that every tariff argument has the same shape as a war on the sun.

question: Socrates asks Euthyphro: are holy things holy because the gods love them, or do the gods love them because they are holy? Why is the fork uncomfortable?
answer: If divine love makes a thing holy, morality is arbitrary; if the gods see prior holiness, good stands above them.
choices: If divine love makes a thing holy, morality is arbitrary; if the gods see prior holiness, good stands above them.
If gods agreed on holiness, the matter would close; their endless quarrels make every human verdict guesswork.
If holiness is a single thing, every act is wholly holy or not; with degrees, no act is ever fully pious.
If piety is taught at home, each city has its own gods; if known by reason, the gods of all peoples are one.
context: The dilemma is staged outside the courthouse before Socrates' own trial. Either horn costs believers something: divine authorship of morality, or moral standards more fundamental than divinity. Aquinas and later theologians have spent centuries trying to slip between the horns.

question: Socrates told the jury his daimon — an inner voice that had guided him since childhood — had never warned him against coming to court. The strangest thing was what the voice would never do, even when he wanted it to. What was that?
answer: It only said no — pulling him back from wrong action, never telling him what to do; conscience as veto, not as positive command.
choices: It only said no — pulling him back from wrong action, never telling him what to do; conscience as veto, not as positive command.
It only spoke during sleep — awake, he reasoned through choices like any Athenian citizen facing a difficult decision.
It only spoke on civic matters — about private moral questions the daimon kept silent, leaving him to ordinary judgment.
It only spoke about other people's plans — about his own intentions, the voice would always stay mute and useless.
context: Socrates told the jury the daimon had not stopped him from coming to court — confirmation, he said, that what looked like disaster somehow was not. A purely negative oracle is philosophically odd: it constrains action without supplying a positive vision of the good. The view treats conscience as a restraining principle — the moral life is built from refusals, while positive choice remains the work of ordinary reasoning.

question: Friends came to Socrates' cell with a bribed guard and an escape route. He refused. In the Crito, his reason was not courage — something else he owed Athens. What was it?
answer: He had benefited from Athens' laws all his life; breaking them now would undermine the rule he had agreed to.
choices: He had benefited from Athens' laws all his life; breaking them now would undermine the rule he had agreed to.
The gods had arranged the verdict from the start, and a wise man bends to fate rather than fighting its course.
Fleeing would only delay worse punishment from above, since the gods cared more for impiety than for sentencing.
His friends would face certain reprisal once he was gone; no philosopher buys his life with others' suffering.
context: The Crito gives Western political philosophy one of its earliest social-contract arguments. Socrates personifies the Laws of Athens: you ate our bread, raised children under us, stayed when you could have left. To break us is to be the kind of person you've argued against.

question: Socrates compared himself not to a teacher but to a midwife — his mother's trade. He insisted he had no wisdom of his own to deliver. What did the comparison capture about how his questioning worked?
answer: He produced no ideas himself; he drew out what others already believed, then tested whether the belief survived.
choices: He produced no ideas himself; he drew out what others already believed, then tested whether the belief survived.
He worked alongside the one reasoning, sharing the labor of thought as a midwife shared a mother's labor.
He took no payment, just as a midwife served poor women who could not afford a doctor's fees themselves.
He waited for the right moment, as a midwife waited for the body's readiness, never forcing things early.
context: The midwife image runs through the Theaetetus. The Socratic 'I know nothing' is not false modesty: it is the working condition of the method. A midwife who herself gives birth on the labor-room floor cannot help anyone else.

question: The Delphic oracle said no one in Athens was wiser than Socrates. He felt he knew nothing, so he tried to refute the oracle. His conclusion was darker than flattering.
answer: Others reputed wise were as ignorant as he, but did not know it; his only edge was knowing the size of his ignorance.
choices: Others reputed wise were as ignorant as he, but did not know it; his only edge was knowing the size of his ignorance.
Others reputed wise hid real knowledge from the public, fearing what Athens would do if their doctrines became known.
Others reputed wise knew their crafts but not the gods; he knew the gods but had never mastered any craft at all.
Others reputed wise had bought their reputations with money; he, owning nothing, had never sold truth for standing.
context: From the Apology. Socrates kept questioning poets, politicians, craftsmen — each supposed expert collapsed under three follow-up questions. The oracle's verdict, he decided, was not praise of him but a backhanded indictment of everyone else.

question: In Plato's Cave, prisoners watch shadows on a wall and take them for reality. One escapes, sees the sun, and returns. Plato's twist is in what happens then. What does he say?
answer: They mock him, his eyes ruined for the dark; if they could lay hands on him, they would kill the one freeing them.
choices: They mock him, his eyes ruined for the dark; if they could lay hands on him, they would kill the one freeing them.
They listen in silence, then break their chains one by one, leaving the cave behind and entering the daylight.
They fail to understand his words, since the names he brings back belong to things they have never once seen.
They believe him in part but stay in the cave — judging familiar shadows more comfortable than the climb up.
context: The Republic's most famous image is less about epistemology than politics. The escapee's fate points unmistakably at Socrates: Athens drank the hemlock its own teacher prescribed. Enlightenment, for Plato, is dangerous to whoever brings it home.

question: In Plato's Meno, Socrates walks an uneducated slave boy through doubling a square's area — asking only questions. Plato uses this for a startling conclusion. What is it?
answer: The boy was not learning but remembering; the soul knew the truth before birth, and education recovers what is there.
choices: The boy was not learning but remembering; the soul knew the truth before birth, and education recovers what is there.
The boy was not reasoning but copying; the mind imitates patterns shown to it, so good and bad examples both stick.
The boy was not equal in capacity to a free citizen; what looked like grasp was a trained reflex, not real insight.
The boy was not solving anything himself; Socrates fed every step, and the dialogue made teaching only look real.
context: This is Plato's doctrine of anamnesis — recollection. The soul, having existed before incarnation, has glimpsed the eternal Forms; what we call learning is the slow reawakening of those buried memories. Innate knowledge, two and a half millennia before the modern debate.

question: In Plato's Symposium, Diotima describes love as a ladder. You start with one beautiful body, but the climb forces an unexpected destination. Where does it lead?
answer: Beyond bodies and minds, to Beauty itself — the form everything else has been a partial reflection of all along.
choices: Beyond bodies and minds, to Beauty itself — the form everything else has been a partial reflection of all along.
Beyond mortal attraction altogether, to one god whose perfection makes every human beloved look pale by comparison.
Beyond lover and beloved, to a union of two souls into one — the shared life the highest aim of erotic desire.
Beyond passion into friendship, since steady affection between equals satisfies more than first infatuation can.
context: Diotima's ladder reverses the modern picture of love. Instead of romance as the deepest thing, particular romance is the first rung — the form of Beauty itself is what one is really moving toward, often without knowing it. Plato will not let eros stay small.

question: In Plato's Republic, the soul has three parts — reason, spirit, appetite — and so must the just city. He was not arguing for balance among them. What was his actual claim?
answer: Reason rules, spirit enforces, appetite obeys; injustice is any of the three doing another's work.
choices: Reason rules, spirit enforces, appetite obeys; injustice is any of the three doing another's work.
Reason and appetite negotiate as equals while spirit settles deadlocks between them as needed.
Reason yields to spirit when honor demands and to appetite when the body insists; balance is wisdom.
All three vote as equal partners on every action with mandatory unanimity required before doing it.
context: The Republic argues that 'justice' is the same word for two scales: a person whose reason commands and whose passions obey is just, and so is a city in which philosopher-rulers command and producers obey. A radical claim — political and psychological order are literally the same problem.

question: Plato's ideal city depends on what he calls a 'noble lie' told to every citizen from childhood. What was this lie meant to do?
answer: Convince each class that the gods mixed different metals into their souls at birth, so the social order felt natural.
choices: Convince each class that the gods mixed different metals into their souls at birth, so the social order felt natural.
Convince the rulers that an oracle had chosen them rather than a committee, so power felt granted rather than seized.
Convince the soldiers that the gods watched every battle in person, so they fought from divine fear, not love of city.
Convince the people that an old prophecy promised the city's rise, so hardships felt like the cost of shared destiny.
context: Plato calls it a 'noble' lie (gennaion pseudos), but a lie all the same. The myth of the metals — gold, silver, bronze — sorts citizens into rulers, soldiers, and producers. Karl Popper would later read this as a founding document of authoritarian politics. Plato thought he was preventing tyranny.

question: In Plato's Phaedo, Socrates spends his last hours arguing that his friends should not weep — because death is good. What was his central argument?
answer: The soul is immortal and the body has blocked its view of truth; death frees the soul to know the eternal Forms.
choices: The soul is immortal and the body has blocked its view of truth; death frees the soul to know the eternal Forms.
The soul is fine atoms that escape the body at death and enter a new being shaped by the previous life.
The soul does not survive, but a life of wisdom is already complete; nothing is owed to one who reasoned well.
The soul belongs to the gods, who recall it at the appointed hour; resisting that summons would be impiety.
context: The Phaedo's dying-day setting is part of the argument. Socrates is calm because his philosophy commits him to be — fear of death, on this view, betrays an attachment to embodiment the lover of wisdom should have outgrown long ago. Whether his actual friends were consoled is another question.

question: Aristotle held that we become brave by doing brave acts — virtue is built by repetition. But he was not just claiming actions become reflex; the inner life changes too. What was the deeper claim?
answer: Habit reshapes appetite itself; the trained person feels pleasure in right action — desire is remade.
choices: Habit reshapes appetite itself; the trained person feels pleasure in right action — desire is remade.
Habit replaces reason in time; the trained person stops deliberating and acts on skilled reflex alone.
Habit lets the soul recall the Forms it knew before birth; virtue is recovery of innate pattern.
Habit teaches the body to obey what the mind already grasps; virtue closes the gap from within.
context: Aristotle's word is hexis — a settled disposition. The Spartan boy made to share his food finds sharing easy in time; the courageous soldier feels fear and acts well anyway, then someday no longer needs the second step. Virtue lived in is virtue altered.

question: Aristotle's doctrine of the mean places virtue between two vices — courage between rashness and cowardice. What did he warn was the most common mistake?
answer: Reading the mean as an exact midpoint between extremes, when it is the right amount for this person now — a moving target.
choices: Reading the mean as an exact midpoint between extremes, when it is the right amount for this person now — a moving target.
Reading the mean as the moderate option always, when in real emergencies it is better to overshoot than err on caution.
Reading the mean as something anyone can find, when only the rare wise statesman has standing to identify it for others.
Reading the mean as a rule for actions, when Aristotle meant it for the feelings beneath — emotions must be moderate.
context: Aristotle is explicit: the mean is not 'the same for everyone.' A wrestler eats more than a clerk; the courage of a soldier is not the courage of a child. Mistaking the mean for an arithmetic average has produced centuries of cardboard Aristotelianism.

question: Aristotle said a full explanation needs four causes: material (bronze), formal (shape), efficient (sculptor), final. What did he mean by the fourth?
answer: The end or purpose a thing is for — the goal explaining why it came to be; nature, he held, has goals as well as causes.
choices: The end or purpose a thing is for — the goal explaining why it came to be; nature, he held, has goals as well as causes.
The last event in the chain — the final push that finished the work, set apart from earlier pushes that only partly mattered.
The eternal pattern the thing imitates — the perfect form it strives to match, which alone determines a true example.
The hidden underlying agent — the unseen force behind the others, which philosophy and not observation can reveal.
context: Final causes — telos — are what later science threw out. A stone falls, for Aristotle, because earth seeks its place; for Newton, because of gravity, full stop. Aristotle's purposive universe died slowly, and biology is still arguing about whether it should ever have left.

question: Aristotle distinguished three kinds of friendship — utility, pleasure, virtue. Only the third was full. The difference was not what they shared, but what they loved in each other. What did he say it was?
answer: Utility and pleasure friends love what they get; virtue friends love the other's character itself.
choices: Utility and pleasure friends love what they get; virtue friends love the other's character itself.
Utility and pleasure friends love a shared project; virtue friends love a mission that outlasts them.
Utility and pleasure friends love each other privately; virtue friends love openly before the city.
Utility and pleasure friends arise in youth, when people change; virtue friends arise when settled.
context: Aristotle's typology cuts close to the bone. Most modern relationships, he would say, are friendships of utility or pleasure dressed up as more — and there is nothing wrong with that, as long as no one mistakes the dressing for the thing. Virtue friendship he thought rare, slow, and lifelong.

question: Aristotle called humans the 'political animal' — zoon politikon. This was not about caring for politics. It was a metaphysical claim. What did he mean?
answer: A human apart from the polis is not yet fully human; we complete our nature only in a community of laws and speech.
choices: A human apart from the polis is not yet fully human; we complete our nature only in a community of laws and speech.
A human is factional by instinct; we form parties and rivalries as wolves form packs — politics is unavoidable.
A human is ruled by ambition over other appetites; honor-seeking in public is the single deepest motive we have.
A human only flourishes under good rulers; we are dependent creatures whose virtue rises with the city's leaders.
context: Aristotle's point is steeper than 'humans are social.' Bees are social. He means that without polis — law, deliberation, the back-and-forth of public reason — a human being is not yet what a human being is. A man outside the city, he says, is either a beast or a god.

question: Aristotle's Poetics asks why people pay to watch terrible things on stage. Tragedy, he said, works by katharsis. What was his actual claim about how this works?
answer: The audience feels real pity and fear at safe distance; the experience purges those emotions, leaving viewers calmer.
choices: The audience feels real pity and fear at safe distance; the experience purges those emotions, leaving viewers calmer.
The audience identifies with the hero's choices; learning from his ruin, they leave the theater wiser about pride.
The audience watches the gods enforce moral law; seeing wickedness punished, they grow committed to the city's justice.
The audience sees a craft they cannot do; admiring the artistry, they leave with refined taste rather than feeling.
context: Katharsis is one of the most contested words in ancient philosophy. Aristotle's metaphor is medical — purgation, clearing — not moral. Watching Oedipus tear out his eyes is supposed to drain the audience of an excess they carried in, not to teach a lesson about humility. Theory has been arguing with him ever since.

question: Epicurus wrote out a 'four-part cure' that his followers were told to memorize like a basic medicine. What four fears did he say it dissolves?
answer: Fear of the gods, fear of death, fear that good is unreachable, and fear that pain cannot be borne.
choices: Fear of the gods, fear of death, fear that good is unreachable, and fear that pain cannot be borne.
Fear of poverty, fear of illness, fear that friendship is fragile, and fear that pleasure must be earned.
Fear of error, fear of shame, fear that the world is hostile, and fear that the soul will be punished.
Fear of tyrants, fear of exile, fear that virtue brings danger, and fear that the city cannot be trusted.
context: Epicureans called it the tetrapharmakos — gods are not to be feared, death is not to be felt, the good is easy to get, the terrible is easy to endure. A medicine cabinet for the mind, recited until it became reflex.

question: Lucretius taught that atoms fall through the void. But if every atom fell in perfectly parallel lines, nothing could ever happen. What rescue did he propose?
answer: An unpredictable swerve — atoms now and then deviate slightly, so collisions, worlds, and choice become possible.
choices: An unpredictable swerve — atoms now and then deviate slightly, so collisions, worlds, and choice become possible.
A guiding intellect — some divine mind nudges atoms into the patterns the visible cosmos requires for order.
A primal vortex — the original whirling motion of matter explains why parallel paths could never have held.
A web of attractions — atoms pull on one another so parallel falling is broken by their natural affinities.
context: The clinamen, or swerve, was Lucretius and Epicurus's most controversial physics. Cicero mocked it as causeless motion. Defenders said it was what saved the universe from a frozen, pointless rain.

question: Epicurus taught that the gods exist and live in perfect bliss between the worlds. Yet he said you should never pray to them. Why not?
answer: Their bliss depends on troubling about nothing — so a god who answered prayers would not be a god at all.
choices: Their bliss depends on troubling about nothing — so a god who answered prayers would not be a god at all.
Their substance is too refined to register human voices — words must reach the divine through matched offerings.
Their love is so universal that singling one mortal out for help would be a cruelty to all the others.
Their power is bounded by fate — even the highest god cannot grant what the cosmic order has not allowed.
context: For Epicurus, calm was the mark of divinity. A god who managed the world or punished the wicked would be perpetually anxious — which is exactly what the gods, being gods, cannot be. The cure: stop expecting them to mind your business.

question: Epicurus wrote: 'When death is present, we are not; when we are present, death is not.' What conclusion did he draw from this little argument?
answer: Death is nothing to us — it is never an experience anyone undergoes, and the time after we die is no worse than the eternity before we were born.
choices: Death is nothing to us — it is never an experience anyone undergoes, and the time after we die is no worse than the eternity before we were born.
Death is the soul's gentle release — what frightens us is the body's stubborn reluctance to let the soul go free at the parting of the two.
Death is a passage to judgment — the wise person learns to fear not death itself but the verdict that waits beyond it for every human soul.
Death is unknown to us — what frightens us is the silence of the gods about what really happens after the last breath has gone out.
context: The argument is starkly simple: pain and joy are experiences; an experience requires someone to have it; the dead are no one. Lucretius later extended it with the symmetry move — the eternity before your birth was no calamity, and the eternity after your death has the same shape; the two non-existences mirror each other, and one is not feared because it is not yours to undergo.

question: Epictetus opened his Handbook with a single sorting rule any student had to master first. What were the two boxes he sorted everything into?
answer: Things up to us — judgment, desire, action — and things not up to us, like body, wealth, reputation.
choices: Things up to us — judgment, desire, action — and things not up to us, like body, wealth, reputation.
Things the gods govern — fate, fortune, weather — and things mortals govern, like household, trade, oath.
Things the body suffers — hunger, cold, pain — and things the soul suffers, like envy, grief, longing.
Things one ought to do — duty, oath, care — and things one only might do, like leisure, art, friendly visits.
context: The Stoic dichotomy of control. Epictetus said almost all human misery comes from confusing the two — trying to control what we cannot, neglecting what we can. The slave-born teacher built his whole ethics on this distinction.

question: Marcus Aurelius told himself to picture Rome from far above — rooftops, markets, armies, parties — until everything looked small. What did the Stoics say this was for?
answer: To shrink your private quarrels and ambitions back to their real size against the scale of the whole cosmos.
choices: To shrink your private quarrels and ambitions back to their real size against the scale of the whole cosmos.
To learn the city's geography so that, in a crisis of office, the statesman can move armies without delay.
To prepare the soul for its release at death, when it will look down on the body it has finally left behind.
To detach from politics entirely, since the Stoic sage withdraws from civic life to tend the inner citadel.
context: The Stoics called it the view from above — a deliberate widening of perspective. The trick is that nothing visible from that height stays as urgent as it felt from inside. Modern astronauts have reported the same effect from orbit.

question: Seneca told his friend Lucilius to spend a few minutes each morning rehearsing the day's disasters — shipwreck, exile, a child's death. What was the point?
answer: To rob the worst events of their shock — a misfortune already imagined cuts shallower when it arrives.
choices: To rob the worst events of their shock — a misfortune already imagined cuts shallower when it arrives.
To inspire urgent action — the man who pictures ruin clearly will work harder to keep his household secure.
To purify desire by exposure — naming each loss strips its hold on the mind until none of it pulls anymore.
To appease the unseen powers — by speaking the worst aloud, the wise turn the gods' attention elsewhere.
context: Premeditatio malorum — premeditation of evils. The Stoics thought sudden grief came from unprepared minds, not from the events themselves. A father who has already pictured his child's death does not love the child less; he is just no longer ambushed.

question: The Stoics held that the wise person aims at apatheia. Translators warn this is NOT what English speakers hear in the word. What did Stoics actually mean?
answer: Freedom from the destructive passions — fear, greed, rage — not the absence of love, joy, or rational concern.
choices: Freedom from the destructive passions — fear, greed, rage — not the absence of love, joy, or rational concern.
Withdrawal from civic life — the sage retires from politics entirely to attend solely to the inner citadel.
Total indifference to others — the wise person feels neither pity nor delight at what happens to anyone else.
Calm acceptance of ignorance — the sage suspends judgment on every question that reason cannot fully settle.
context: Modern 'apathy' is a Stoic word with the meaning sandblasted off. The Stoic sage felt friendship, civic duty, and 'good feelings' like rational joy; what they refused were the disordered passions that warp judgment.

question: Crates the Cynic gave away his fortune to live in rags. The aristocrat Hipparchia married him, then joined him sleeping and eating in the open agora. The marriage was a deliberate demonstration. Of what?
answer: That a virtuous life and a real marriage need no property, status, or privacy at all.
choices: That a virtuous life and a real marriage need no property, status, or privacy at all.
That a woman could match any man in argument — Hipparchia debating philosophers as proof.
That romantic love is the highest of human goods, exceeding every other claim on a life.
That children belong to all — Cynic adults would raise any offspring as a shared ward.
context: Crates and Hipparchia were ancient Athens's most scandalous philosophical marriage. They lived, ate, and conducted married life openly in the agora — putting Cynic shamelessness (anaideia) on display as a kind of moral demonstration.

question: Diogenes called his routine askesis — training, like an athlete's. He walked barefoot in winter, hugged bronze statues in summer, begged from people he knew would refuse. Why?
answer: To harden the soul against fortune — one who practices loss in small doses cannot be ruined by larger.
choices: To harden the soul against fortune — one who practices loss in small doses cannot be ruined by larger.
To shame the wealthy — public displays of want were calculated insults to the comfortable men of Athens.
To purge the body's gross humors — Cynics held that physical hardship rebalances the soul's physiology.
To gather followers by spectacle — Diogenes was building a school, and theatrical poverty drew the pupil.
context: Cynicism took its name from the Greek for 'dog' — the Cynic lived plainly, like an animal that knows what it really needs. Askesis is the same root the word 'ascetic' grew from, but for the Cynics it was muscle-training for freedom, not piety.

question: Pyrrho went with Alexander's army to India, met local sages, came home with a strange practice: never affirming or denying anything firmly. What followed, he said?
answer: A deep calm settled over him — when no opinion is gripped tightly, no opinion can disturb its holder.
choices: A deep calm settled over him — when no opinion is gripped tightly, no opinion can disturb its holder.
A keen new sight opened — when opinion was set aside, the world appeared as it truly is for the first time.
A close bond with the gods — for Pyrrho, suspending judgment was the only honest worship of beings beyond.
A clear sense of duty — once private opinion fell silent, the voice of common custom alone showed the way.
context: Pyrrho's Skepticism was a therapy, not just an epistemology. Epoche — suspension of judgment — produced ataraxia, untroubled calm. His followers called it the discovery of the Hellenistic age: peace of mind through letting go of all your firm convictions.

question: Stoics, Epicureans, and Pyrrhonian Skeptics offered students roughly the same prize at the end of philosophy: different routes, one destination. What did all three aim at?
answer: Ataraxia — an unshakable calm that no fortune, no loss, no quarrel could disturb in the wise soul.
choices: Ataraxia — an unshakable calm that no fortune, no loss, no quarrel could disturb in the wise soul.
Eudaimonia — the full flourishing of a complete human life lived well over time in a well-ordered city.
Apocatastasis — the soul's eventual restoration to its divine origin once it has been purified of matter.
Henosis — a final mystical union with the One, in which the philosopher's individual mind is absorbed.
context: The Hellenistic age was an age of empire, exile, and lost cities. The schools competed fiercely on doctrine but converged on the goal: a soul that could not be ruined from outside. Their disagreements were about which road actually got you there.

question: Epicureans called wealth, fame, and political office 'natural but unnecessary' — or vain and dangerous. One good they treated as essential and worth the trouble. What was it?
answer: Friendship — a small circle of close, trusted companions who would stand by you when fortune turned bad.
choices: Friendship — a small circle of close, trusted companions who would stand by you when fortune turned bad.
Family — the household into which one is born sets the lifelong limits of duty, affection, and honor.
Citizenship — the engaged civic life remains the highest training the city offers a soul that wants joy.
Solitude — only the philosopher who withdraws from human company can master the discipline fortune demands.
context: Epicurus's Garden was a community. He wrote that of all the goods wisdom provides for the happy life, by far the greatest is friendship. The garden welcomed women and slaves at a time when neither was welcome in most schools — a fact Romans found suspicious for centuries.

question: Laozi argued that a clay pot, a wheel hub, and an empty room share one feature that makes each one useful. What did he say it was?
answer: The empty space inside — usefulness comes from absence, not from the material surrounding it
choices: The empty space inside — usefulness comes from absence, not from the material surrounding it
The skilled craft of the maker who shapes raw material into a precise and functional form
The natural function of clay, wood, and stone, which determines the purpose each can serve
The harmony between maker and material, achieved when neither dominates the creative act
context: Daodejing Chapter 11. Thirty spokes share one hub: the empty space at the center is what makes the wheel turn. Clay is molded into a vessel: the empty space inside is what holds the water. Doors and windows are cut in a wall: the empty space is what makes the room livable. Laozi was making a general philosophical point — what is absent is often what does the work, and a culture that fixates on what is there will miss what is not there.

question: Laozi wrote that the best ruler is one whose people barely know exists — yet at the end of his reign they look around and say 'we did this ourselves.' He called it wu wei. What kind of rule is it?
answer: Wu wei — accomplishing without forcing; the ruler removes obstacles, the people do the doing.
choices: Wu wei — accomplishing without forcing; the ruler removes obstacles, the people do the doing.
Ren — leading by visible moral example, so subjects watching the ruler are inspired to imitate.
Li — performing each role in the social order with care, sincerity, and the proper deference.
Fa — strict laws applied identically to everyone, holding the state together by force of rule.
context: Daodejing Chapter 17. Laozi's political claim is sharper than it first sounds — he is not endorsing weak government but criticizing the activist ruler who believes constant intervention improves things. Compare the three classical rivals: Confucian li (ritual roles), Confucian ren (moral example), and Legalist fa (strict law). Hayek made a structurally similar argument 2,400 years later.

question: Among the Confucians, the admirable person was the polished scholar — schooled, ritually trained, ornamented by years of study. Laozi pointed to the opposite: pu, the uncarved block of wood. Why was that the higher ideal?
answer: The uncarved block still holds every possibility; the polished scholar has been locked into one shape.
choices: The uncarved block still holds every possibility; the polished scholar has been locked into one shape.
The uncarved block has memorized every text and ritual the tradition has ever produced over time.
The uncarved block has trained each latent talent to its fullest through long, disciplined effort.
The uncarved block has renounced ordinary life and withdrawn entirely from all social attachment.
context: Pu (樸) recurs across the Daodejing (Ch. 15, 19, 28, 32, 37, 57). The block is wood that still holds every possibility because the carver has not yet locked it into one shape.
