context: Hume's puzzle was empirical: we see succession but never the connecting tie. Kant agreed we never observe causation as a quality of things, then turned the question around. Without a causal rule the mind itself supplies, no sequence could even be perceived as objective.

question: Kant compared his move to what Copernicus did in astronomy. The comparison sounds boastful, yet he meant it modestly. How was the turn really a humbling?
answer: It dropped the ambition to know things in themselves and asked only what conditions a mind must meet for experience.
choices: It dropped the ambition to know things in themselves and asked only what conditions a mind must meet for experience.
It admitted earlier philosophers had been correct about reality and merely organized truths already discovered.
It conceded that revelation must complete what philosophy can only begin, returning reason to a medieval role.
It accepted that science would eventually replace philosophy and provided a stopgap until science took over.
context: Copernicus did not enlarge the heavens; he relocated the observer. Kant likewise did not extend metaphysics; he asked what minds like ours must contribute for any object to appear to us at all. The turn was a confession of limits, and those limits proved to be what made objective experience possible.

question: Take an ordinary judgment: 'the flower is red.' Aristotle's logic treats red as a property belonging to a thing called the flower. The Kyoto-school philosopher Nishida said this gets it backwards. He called his alternative basho — Japanese for 'place' or 'field.' What was his move?
answer: Redness is not owned by a thing; it shows up in a field (vision, then consciousness, then absolute nothingness). The thing is what the field makes visible, not what carries the property.
choices: Redness is not owned by a thing; it shows up in a field (vision, then consciousness, then absolute nothingness). The thing is what the field makes visible, not what carries the property.
Redness still belongs to a substance — basho is just a new Japanese name for the underlying bearer Aristotle already identified, with the logic of subject and predicate left untouched.
Redness has its meaning only inside the public practice of language — basho is the social space where colour-claims get used, with no deeper ground beyond shared practice.
Redness is a moment in absolute spirit unfolding through history — basho is Hegel's developing whole rendered into Japanese vocabulary, with the dialectic running underneath.
context: Basho inverts subject-logic. A red flower is not a substance bearing redness; redness shows in a field of vision, set in consciousness, set in absolute nothingness (zettai mu). Aristotelian substance, Wittgensteinian language-games, and Hegelian spirit are real rivals — basho is none, and the nothingness is not the absolute whole.

question: Nishitani thought Europe had not yet thought nihilism — the loss of meaning — through to the end. He answered from sunyata, the Mahayana idea of emptiness: no thing has a self-contained nature. Look at a pine tree. What does emptiness do to it, and so to nihilism?
answer: It passes through nihilism. The pine loses its look of being self-grounded; on the far side of that loss it returns as itself — just the pine, with nothing propping it up.
choices: It passes through nihilism. The pine loses its look of being self-grounded; on the far side of that loss it returns as itself — just the pine, with nothing propping it up.
It refuses nihilism from the start. Buddhist metaphysics already holds the ground the West lost in modernity, so the European problem simply never arises with real force on Buddhist soil.
It accepts nihilism as final. The noble individual must create meaning where the indifferent world offers none — in the style of the Paris existentialists writing through the cafés.
It treats nihilism as a passing social mood. Modernity disenchanted ritual life; the cure is renewed communal practice and shared liturgy, not a metaphysical move into emptiness.
context: Religion and Nothingness (1961). Nishitani read Nietzsche, Heidegger, and the Mahayana sunyata literature together. Not refutation but transit: at the standpoint of emptiness, the pine is no self-grounded thing, and just so the pine is wholly the pine. The apologetic, Sartrean, and sociological distractors are real responses — none Nishitani's.

question: Two schools, separated by language and centuries: the Greek Pyrrhonist skeptics aimed at ataraxia — untroubled calm — by suspending all metaphysical judgment. The Indian Madhyamaka Buddhists aimed at peace through emptiness — the view that no thing has a fixed self-nature. Different worlds, same therapeutic shape. What did the two methods share?
answer: Suspension itself was the cure. The mind quiets when it stops insisting on essences. Peace follows from letting metaphysical claims go — not from finding the right one.
choices: Suspension itself was the cure. The mind quiets when it stops insisting on essences. Peace follows from letting metaphysical claims go — not from finding the right one.
Both reached the certainty that nothing exists at all; it is the radical denial of being itself that brings the practitioner peace at last.
Both held that ordinary perception is wholly reliable; the disputes that disturb the mind are caused only by careless use of philosophical jargon.
Both grounded their peace in a positive metaphysics of the One; tranquility comes from contact with the single substance behind appearances.
context: Sextus Empiricus described epoche — suspension of assent — producing ataraxia. Nagarjuna's catuskoti refused all four positions on inherent existence; emptiness is not a thesis but release from theses. Philosophy as therapy.

question: Solzhenitsyn left Russia on the morning of his arrest with one essay ready. It asked nothing heroic of ordinary citizens. What single demand did it make?
answer: A citizen need not protest in the streets, only refuse to repeat in his own voice what he knows is a lie.
choices: A citizen need not protest in the streets, only refuse to repeat in his own voice what he knows is a lie.
Every honest citizen owes the regime open dissent, since silence under tyranny is collaboration with it.
A citizen must withdraw entirely from public life, accepting internal exile until the regime collapses.
The moral task is to convert one neighbor each year, building a network that can speak when time comes.
context: Live Not by Lies, published the day Solzhenitsyn was expelled in February 1974, set the minimum bar deliberately low. Not heroism. Not martyrdom. Only the refusal to sign your name to what you know is false. He thought a regime built on universal assent could not survive even that small subtraction.

question: Marx asked where profit comes from in a system where, on average, equal values trade for equal values. His answer turned on one peculiar commodity. Which?
answer: Labor-power — the worker's capacity to work, sold by the day but producing more value than its day's wage.
choices: Labor-power — the worker's capacity to work, sold by the day but producing more value than its day's wage.
Land rent — the natural fertility of the soil, charged for by the owner without any labor on his own part.
Skilled craft — the rare ability of the trained worker, paid above the unskilled rate by long custom of guilds.
Money capital — the loaned sum itself, returning more than it began with by virtue of interest charged in time.
context: Marx granted Smith and Ricardo the puzzle: if every trade is even, no one should get richer. His move was to distinguish labor (the work done) from labor-power (the capacity to do it). The capitalist buys the capacity for a wage that covers a day's subsistence; the worker in that day produces more value than the wage. The gap was surplus value — where, in Marx's model, profit lived.

question: Hegel's dialectic — development through contradiction, where opposing tendencies generate a new form — was his account of how ideas and history move. Engels in Dialectics of Nature (1870s, pub. 1925) extended it into the physical world. What central claim did he defend?
answer: Nature itself develops through contradiction: heat water enough and a quantitative change (rising temperature) yields a qualitative one (becoming steam) — dialectic at work in matter.
choices: Nature itself develops through contradiction: heat water enough and a quantitative change (rising temperature) yields a qualitative one (becoming steam) — dialectic at work in matter.
Nature is fundamentally mechanical: every change at every scale reduces to the motion of matter under fixed Newtonian laws, with no deeper pattern at work in chemistry or biology.
Nature is teleological: each species, mineral, and force aims at an end set for it in the rational order of beings, and the task of natural science is patiently to trace that order.
Nature is layered: each level of organization (atomic, chemical, biological) adds powers not derivable from the level beneath, but no contradiction is at work in any upward step.
context: Engels wrote Dialectics of Nature in the 1870s but left it unpublished; it appeared only in 1925. He drew examples from chemistry, biology, and physics — water heated through a threshold becomes steam, a seed negates itself in the plant, the plant in the seed — and argued the dialectical pattern Hegel had seen in thought was at work in matter. Later philosophers of science have contested the move sharply.

question: Nagarjuna ran a four-cornered move called the catuskoti or tetralemma: for any claim P he would refute P, then not-P, then both, then neither. What was the point of running every option to ruin?
answer: To show that every fixed position about ultimate reality breaks down and must be released, not replaced by a fifth.
choices: To show that every fixed position about ultimate reality breaks down and must be released, not replaced by a fifth.
To eliminate three of the four corners so the one surviving option could be safely affirmed as the correct answer.
To prove that the law of non-contradiction fails in the East, where Aristotelian logic was never developed at all.
To classify metaphysical claims into four neat families so a debater could quickly identify an opponents view.
context: The catuskoti (four corners) appears throughout the Mulamadhyamakakarika. Nagarjuna applies it to causation, motion, the self, even nirvana — each time arguing that none of the four can stand without contradiction. The conclusion is not that some fifth view wins; it is that the question presupposes inherent existence (svabhava) and dissolves once that presupposition does. The elimination-method, anti-logic, and taxonomy distractors are real misreadings — particularly the first, common in early Western scholarship.

question: The fourth-century Yogacara school summed up its position as cittamatra — mind-only. Rivals heard solipsism. What were Vasubandhu and Asanga actually claiming?
answer: What we take as outer objects is built by mental processes; the analysis is about appearance, not other minds.
choices: What we take as outer objects is built by mental processes; the analysis is about appearance, not other minds.
Only one mind exists, and every other apparent mind is a projection that mind has generated within itself.
Matter exists but cannot be known directly; the mind copies what is out there, and the copy is what we meet.
Mind and matter are two aspects of one neutral substance; the appearance of difference is itself a mental effect.
context: Yogacara — also called Cittamatra or Vijnanavada — emerges with Asanga and his half-brother Vasubandhu in the fourth century. Their claim concerns the structure of experience: every object we encounter has already been processed by perception, conception, and karmic predisposition. They were not denying other minds (that was the Madhyamaka-leaning critique of them) and not denying matter outright (that was Berkeley's later position, structurally distinct). The dual-aspect distractor is Spinoza's view, a real rival from a much later tradition.

question: Wittgenstein closed his Tractatus with a strange instruction: the reader who has understood his sentences must finally recognize them as nonsensical and throw them away — "kick the ladder down" after climbing it. What did he mean about his own book?
answer: Its sentences violate its own theory of meaningful language, so they work only as a ladder to a view that cannot itself be stated
choices: It is a draft that he intended to revise once symbolic logic had matured enough to express its claims rigorously and properly
Its sentences violate its own theory of meaningful language, so they work only as a ladder to a view that cannot itself be stated
It is meant as deliberate parody of metaphysics, showing every philosophical sentence ever written collapses into pure technical nonsense
Its propositions are true only for the author and become false the moment any other reader tries to make philosophical use of them
context: Tractatus 6.54 — the famous "ladder" passage. Wittgenstein's picture theory says only sentences depicting possible facts are meaningful; but his own sentences are about the logical form of meaning itself, not facts. So by his own lights they are nonsense — yet useful nonsense, like a ladder you discard after climbing. This self-undermining structure is what distinguishes the Tractatus from ordinary metaphysics.

question: The early Wittgenstein claimed sentences "picture" facts. A picture and what it depicts must share something for the picture to work at all. What did he say a meaningful sentence shares with the fact it describes?
answer: Logical form — the same pattern of elements standing in the same relations, like a model of a car crash mirroring the crash itself
choices: A common vocabulary of names, so every object in the fact has exactly one corresponding word in the sentence describing the world
Logical form — the same pattern of elements standing in the same relations, like a model of a car crash mirroring the crash itself
A shared causal history, since the sentence must have been produced by the very fact whose existence the sentence then reports
A verifying observation, because no sentence has meaning until some observer has confirmed the fact it claims actually obtains
context: Tractatus 2.1–3.3. Wittgenstein was reportedly inspired by a Paris courtroom using toy cars to reconstruct an accident: the toys aren't the cars, but the spatial arrangement matches. A proposition relates to a fact the same way — not by naming or causing, but by having the same logical structure. This was meant to dissolve metaphysical puzzles by exposing them as sentences that have no possible logical-form match.

question: Wittgenstein wrote that ethics "cannot be put into words." He didn't mean ethics is unreal — quite the opposite. Why did his picture theory force this strange conclusion about moral claims?
answer: Ethical statements try to say what the world should be, but propositions can only picture how it is — value lies outside what language can depict
choices: Moral language describes feelings rather than facts, so ethical sentences are technically meaningless emotional outbursts rather than genuine claims at all
Ethics depends on God's commands, and statements about God lie beyond the natural world that scientific propositions are competent to describe accurately
Ethical statements try to say what the world should be, but propositions can only picture how it is — value lies outside what language can depict
Moral terms shift meaning across cultures, so no universal proposition could ever capture an ethical fact that holds for everyone everywhere alike
context: Tractatus 6.42–6.421. For Wittgenstein, propositions are pictures of possible states of affairs — they say how things stand. "Murder is wrong" tries to say something else: how things ought to stand. That isn't picturable. He concluded ethics is "transcendental" — it shows itself in how a life is lived, not in what can be said. Crucially, he held ethics is *more* important than the sayable, not less.

question: "Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent" — the closing line of the Tractatus. The Vienna Circle read it as dismissing metaphysics. Wittgenstein was furious. What did he say the silence actually honors?
answer: Ethics, aesthetics, and the meaning of life — the most important things, which show themselves but cannot be stated as propositions
choices: Empirical science, since only scientific claims meet the strict logical requirements that propositional language must satisfy to count as sensible
Ethics, aesthetics, and the meaning of life — the most important things, which show themselves but cannot be stated as propositions
Religion specifically, which he regarded as refined superstition that polite philosophical conversation ought to pass over and leave without comment
Personal experience, because subjective states are private and so any attempt to put them into shared public language must necessarily distort them
context: Tractatus 7. Wittgenstein wrote to his publisher that the unwritten half of the book was the important half — "that which I have not written." The Vienna Circle read him as a fellow positivist saying metaphysics is nonsense and good riddance. He insisted they had it backward: silence about the highest things is reverence for them, not dismissal of them.

question: Wittgenstein asked what all games share — chess, solitaire, ring-a-ring-a-roses, Olympic sport. He found no single feature shared by every game. What did this show about most concepts?
answer: They are held together by overlapping similarities like family resemblances — not by a hidden essence every instance of the concept must share
choices: They are held together by overlapping similarities like family resemblances — not by a hidden essence every instance of the concept must share
They are vague because ordinary language evolved without scientific precision, but careful philosophical analysis can in principle yield sharp definitions
They cluster around a single prototypical case, and other instances count as members by their measurable degree of similarity to that prototype
They are cultural constructs with no extension in reality — a word like "game" picks out no genuine kind, only a contingent grouping of practices
context: Philosophical Investigations §§66–71. The point is aimed at the Socratic-Platonic search for the "essence" of justice, beauty, knowledge — the assumption every meaningful word must name a hidden common feature. Wittgenstein: look closely and you find a network of overlapping similarities, like the way siblings share features without any single feature being common to all of them. No essence is needed for the word to work.

question: Wittgenstein wrote that if a lion could speak, we could not understand him. He said understanding language requires sharing "agreement in judgments" — the obvious things. What did he call this bedrock?
answer: A form of life — the web of shared practices, reactions, and unargued certainties on which language users must already agree
choices: Universal grammar — deep linguistic structures common to all human brains, allowing speakers from any culture to translate between languages
A form of life — the web of shared practices, reactions, and unargued certainties on which language users must already agree
Shared symbolic logic — every natural language can be regimented into a single calculus that captures the inferential content of any sentence
A stock of mental concepts — thoughts are private inner objects, and translation matches one speaker's concepts to those of another speaker
context: Philosophical Investigations §§241–242. Wittgenstein's point is that language doesn't rest on more language — it rests on things humans do together: pointing, counting, laughing, mourning, building, eating. A lion's form of life is too different from ours for the shared reactions to obtain, even if its vocal apparatus could produce sentences. "Agreement in judgments" isn't agreement on opinions — it's the prior agreement that lets disagreement on opinions even make sense.

question: Foucault rejected the common picture of power as a thing the strong wield to repress the weak. His provocative claim was that power is productive, not chiefly repressive. What did he say power positively does?
answer: It produces the very subjects, knowledges, and norms through which we understand ourselves and what counts as truth.
choices: It produces the very subjects, knowledges, and norms through which we understand ourselves and what counts as truth.
It distorts a prior natural reason whose recovery, through critique of ideology, would set humanity into freedom.
It expresses, through institutions of the state, the will of whatever class has come to control the means of production.
It manifests, in any community, the deep authority of language whose grammar shapes the speakers who inhabit it.
context: Foucault's wager was that the repressive picture missed the more interesting half of the story. The exam, the medical case file, the personality inventory: each constitutes a kind of subject (the student, the patient, the personality) and a kind of knowledge about them. Power and knowledge are not enemies; they are the same hand seen from two angles.

question: Discipline and Punish opens with a 1757 regicide, drawn and quartered in public, then leaps to a sober 1840 prison timetable: rise at six, work at seven, silence at meals. Foucault was not contrasting cruelty with humanity. What was his genealogical claim about the shift?
answer: A new technology of power had emerged that aimed at the soul through ordered time, not at the body through pain.
choices: A new technology of power had emerged that aimed at the soul through ordered time, not at the body through pain.
A new respect for the dignity of the criminal had emerged among reformers who had read Beccaria and Voltaire well.
A new sense among rulers that the public spectacle of pain had begun to make crowds dangerous, even revolutionary.
A new science of medicine had taught magistrates that prolonged punishment of the body served no rational purpose.
context: Traditional histories told the story as progress: the Enlightenment learned to punish more humanely. Foucault's genealogy turned this around. The timetable was not a softer punishment than the scaffold but a different kind of grip on the person — one that wanted to reach inside and reshape, not just spend its violence on the body and finish.

question: A census taker counting bodies, a vaccination program rolling through a province, a sewer plan drawn over a city map — Foucault dated a shift in the late 18th century when power began acting on populations like this rather than commanding individuals one by one. He called it biopolitics. What was its object and aim?
answer: The life of the population as a whole — its birth rates, health, longevity — managed by statistics and public hygiene.
choices: The life of the population as a whole — its birth rates, health, longevity — managed by statistics and public hygiene.
The conscience of the individual subject — examined, confessed, and corrected by the parish priest or his secular heir.
The political authority of the monarch — gradually shared with parliaments answerable to a propertied middle class.
The legal definition of the citizen — codified in constitutions and bills of rights guaranteeing inalienable liberties.
context: Foucault dated the shift to roughly the late 18th century, when states started counting bodies and tracking causes of death. A census, a vaccination program, a sewer plan: these manage a population rather than command an individual. The right to kill receded; the duty to administer life advanced.

question: Foucault opened History of Sexuality v.1 by mocking the story that Victorians silenced sex and we have been heroically liberating speech about it ever since. He called this the repression hypothesis and turned it on its head. What did he claim had actually happened?
answer: The 19th century produced a vast new discourse on sex through medicine, confession, and law — never less spoken about.
choices: The 19th century produced a vast new discourse on sex through medicine, confession, and law — never less spoken about.
The 19th century produced a real silencing of sex by sermon and statute, which liberal reformers later partly undid.
The 19th century produced no major change in sexual talk, only a shift in which class held the right to publish about it.
The 19th century produced a recovery of ancient erotic candor that had been lost in the long medieval ascetic centuries.
context: Foucault counted the volumes: medical taxonomies of perversion, psychiatric case files, legal codifications, pastoral confession manuals. The Victorians were not silent about sex; they were obsessed with classifying it. The story of repression-and-liberation, he argued, is itself part of the new discourse it pretends to describe.

question: Derrida coined différance — spelled with an 'a' instead of the standard French 'e' in différence. In speech the two are indistinguishable; only the written form shows the change. The French verb différer means both 'to differ' and 'to defer' (postpone). He picked the spelling to enact, not merely assert, what claim about meaning?
answer: A sign's meaning is never present in one moment. It always points sideways — to other signs it differs from — and forward, deferred, to what is yet to come.
choices: A sign's meaning is never present in one moment. It always points sideways — to other signs it differs from — and forward, deferred, to what is yet to come.
A sign's meaning is fixed by the speaker's intention at the moment of utterance; the interpreter's job is to recover what the speaker had in mind.
A sign's meaning is grounded in a stable structure of binary oppositions (light/dark, raw/cooked) that organize a culture's whole vocabulary.
A sign's meaning, used rightly, corresponds to an object or state of affairs the careful speaker can in principle point out in the world.
context: The French verb différer means both to differ and to defer. Derrida coined différance to hold both senses at once, and spelled it so the change shows only on the page. The joke is also the argument: writing, supposedly secondary to speech, turns out to be the only place where the move can even be marked.

question: The Quebec government commissioned Lyotard in 1979 to report on knowledge in computerized societies. His phrase 'incredulity toward metanarratives' — the grand stories of Enlightenment progress and Marxist emancipation — got read as moral verdict. He insisted it was something else. What was his claim?
answer: A descriptive report that, in computerized societies, those grand legitimating stories no longer command working belief.
choices: A descriptive report that, in computerized societies, those grand legitimating stories no longer command working belief.
A normative argument that those grand stories of universal progress had been morally falsified by the wars of the century.
A theological wager that any narrative beyond the parable of the individual soul exceeds what reason can warrant.
A psychological diagnosis that modern subjects, exhausted by ideology, can no longer summon the energy such stories ask.
context: Lyotard's commissioned study was a sociology of knowledge: in technical, information-rich societies, knowledge is justified locally by 'small narratives' tied to performance rather than by appeal to a single universal story. He was not declaring metanarratives wicked. He was reporting that, as a matter of fact, they had stopped doing the legitimating work they once did.

question: Picture a sincere seeker — open to God, looking, finding no belief. Schellenberg's 1993 hiddenness argument: a perfectly loving God would not let such a person stay in the dark. Such people exist. What follows, and how do theists reply?
answer: No such all-loving God exists. Theist replies fall in three families: free will (God lets people resist grace), epistemic distance (faith needs the room hiddenness gives), final reconciliation.
choices: No such all-loving God exists. Theist replies fall in three families: free will (God lets people resist grace), epistemic distance (faith needs the room hiddenness gives), final reconciliation.
The argument suspends itself: 'open to relationship' cannot be defined without circular appeal to the very belief at issue, so the central premise turns out unstable on close inspection.
Hiddenness reveals divine pedagogy at work in formation; theist replies converge on free-will theodicy combined with Hick's soul-making framework as a single unified position, not three.
Hiddenness tells against deism but leaves classical theism untouched; theist replies turn on the difference between a personal and a merely cosmic divinity — only the latter in the dock.
context: Schellenberg's argument is the major hiddenness move in current philosophy of religion. The 1993 version concludes that an all-loving God of the relevant kind does not exist. The three live theistic replies are free-will (resistible grace), epistemic-distance (faith requires hiddenness — John Hick), and universalist (final reconciliation). The distractors scramble those positions in instructive ways.

question: Popper's demarcation rested on logic, not laboratory habit: no number of white swans confirms 'all swans are white,' but one black swan refutes it. From this asymmetry he drew a criterion — for sentences, not scientists. What did it say?
answer: A sentence is scientific to the degree it forbids; the more states of the world its content rules out, the more falsifiable, the more scientific.
choices: A sentence is scientific to the degree it forbids; the more states of the world its content rules out, the more falsifiable, the more scientific.
Scientists should form the habit of attacking their own theories rather than seeking confirming evidence; falsifiability names a research virtue.
A theory becomes scientific only when independent observations confirm its predictions across many distinct experimental conditions (Carnap).
Science requires statistical confirmation; a theory is established once its predictions cross a probabilistic threshold of support (Bayesian).
context: Logic of Scientific Discovery, §6. Popper drew the demarcation in the structure of the statement, not the habits of researchers. 'All swans are white' forbids a black swan; 'history advances dialectically' forbids nothing in particular. The vulgar reading collapses Popper into a research-methodology slogan; his claim was logical — about what makes a sentence scientific at all.

question: Popper said "all swans are white" is scientific even if false. Astrology, by contrast, is unscientific even when its predictions sometimes come true. What does the swan example show about his criterion?
answer: Scientific status concerns what a statement rules out in advance, not whether it is true; astrology survives any outcome through reinterpretation
choices: Science requires precise quantitative predictions; astrology fails because its claims about personality and fate cannot be measured with accuracy
Scientific theories are those produced by accredited researchers using controlled experiments; astrology lacks the institutional setting of real science
Scientific status concerns what a statement rules out in advance, not whether it is true; astrology survives any outcome through reinterpretation
Truth tracks scientific status closely, so the falsity of the swan claim would show that it was not quite scientific in the strict sense Popper meant
context: Conjectures and Refutations, ch. 1. The swan claim risks something specific — one black bird kills it. The astrologer's "a stranger will affect your finances" risks nothing — every life contains strangers and finances. Popper's point is structural: a sentence is scientific by virtue of its prohibitions, regardless of its truth value.

question: Kuhn said normal science is "puzzle-solving" within a framework no one questions. Anomalies accumulate, crisis arrives, revolution happens. What specifically changes when the new paradigm wins?
answer: Standards for what counts as a legitimate problem, a good explanation, and a relevant observation shift together; the old questions stop seeming pressing
choices: A single false prediction is decisively refuted by a crucial experiment, prompting the community to abandon the old theory for its successor
Standards for what counts as a legitimate problem, a good explanation, and a relevant observation shift together; the old questions stop seeming pressing
A more comprehensive theory absorbs the older one as a limiting case, so the previous framework is preserved as an approximation, not overturned
A younger generation of researchers introduces new mathematical tools that finally allow the existing puzzles to be solved with the methods at hand
context: Structure of Scientific Revolutions, chs. 4–9. Newtonian mechanics did not just get replaced; the questions Newtonians cared about (force at a distance) and the ones Einsteinians cared about (frame-relative measurement) are not the same questions. This is not Popper's falsification model — Kuhn argued no single experiment ever forces a paradigm out.

question: Aristotle's 'motion' meant any change toward a thing's natural place — a falling rock, a growing plant. Galileo's 'motion' meant displacement in time. Same word, different worlds. Kuhn called this incommensurability. What did Kuhn claim?
answer: Terms get their meaning from their place in a web of surrounding concepts; change the web and the terms shift with it, leaving no neutral vocabulary above paradigms to translate sentence by sentence.
choices: Terms get their meaning from their place in a web of surrounding concepts; change the web and the terms shift with it, leaving no neutral vocabulary above paradigms to translate sentence by sentence.
Rival paradigms cannot be rationally compared at all; choice between them is settled by preference or social conformity — Feyerabend's stronger move, sometimes miscredited to Kuhn.
Rival paradigms cannot both be true, so a scientific community must collectively decide which to accept by majority vote of working researchers in good methodological standing.
Rival paradigms describe distinct domains of nature that do not really overlap, letting each remain authoritative within its own bounded territory of scientific inquiry.
context: Structure, postscript (1969). Kuhn's point is semantic-holist: scientific terms get their content from their place in the surrounding conceptual web, so changing the paradigm silently changes what the words mean. There is no paradigm-neutral vocabulary to do clean sentence-by-sentence translation. Kuhn denied this meant 'no rational comparison' — that was Feyerabend's stronger move, often miscredited to Kuhn.

question: Lakatos thought Popper was right about demarcation but wrong about where to draw it. The unit of appraisal is not a single theory but a research programme. What separates a progressive from a degenerating one?
answer: A progressive programme keeps predicting novel facts that get confirmed; a degenerating one only patches failures after the fact, predicting nothing new
choices: A progressive programme attracts more researchers and funding over time; a degenerating one slowly loses adherents until no scientist defends it
A progressive programme keeps predicting novel facts that get confirmed; a degenerating one only patches failures after the fact, predicting nothing new
A progressive programme can be derived from accepted prior theories; a degenerating one introduces concepts that contradict established science
A progressive programme uses mathematics rigorously; a degenerating one relies on verbal arguments not precise enough to generate testable predictions
context: Methodology of Scientific Research Programmes, 1970. Lakatos kept Popper's rejection of justificationism but rescued science from naive falsification. Around an unfalsifiable hard core (Newton's laws, say) sits a protective belt of auxiliary hypotheses scientists adjust freely. The honest question is not "was the core falsified?" but "are the belt-adjustments still generating novel predictions, or just saving appearances?"

question: Feyerabend's 1975 Against Method ended in 'anything goes.' Critics read it as 'science is no better than astrology.' He resisted that — called himself a 'flippant Dadaist' — and pointed to the historical record. What was his argument?
answer: Every methodological rule philosophers proposed has been violated by some successful real science; the rules are bad descriptions, not bad practice.
choices: Every methodological rule philosophers proposed has been violated by some successful real science; the rules are bad descriptions, not bad practice.
Science has no special claim to truth; it stands on the same epistemic footing as astrology or any traditional knowledge a culture happens to produce.
Science is a purely social construction in which truth is decided by powerful institutions; methodological talk just disguises academic politics.
Scientists should deliberately drop all methodological constraints in their daily work, since following any rules systematically prevents breakthroughs.
context: Against Method, ch. 1. Feyerabend's argument was historical: Galileo violated the empirical-evidence rule (the tower argument), Bohr violated consistency (electron orbits vs. Maxwell), Einstein violated falsificationism. 'Anything goes' was a sarcastic gloss on the only methodology compatible with the actual record. The strong-relativist reading came later — Feyerabend himself resisted it.

question: Picture choosing a society's basic rules from behind Rawls's 'veil of ignorance' — you don't know whether you'll be rich or poor, healthy or ill, talented or not. Rawls said you would pick maximin: the rule whose worst outcome is least bad. What made this rational, not timid?
answer: Behind the veil you cannot assign probabilities — no way to say how likely you are to end up at the bottom. Without probabilities, the rational move is to insure against the worst case, not gamble.
choices: Behind the veil you cannot assign probabilities — no way to say how likely you are to end up at the bottom. Without probabilities, the rational move is to insure against the worst case, not gamble.
Loss aversion is psychologically universal across cultures, so any rational chooser picks the option that minimizes their later regret over outcomes they have to live with.
Equal initial standing makes any unequal outcome unjust unless every party consents to it from their real-life position once the veil drops and their full identity becomes known.
Self-interest under known probabilities leads parties to bargain for principles that maximize their own expected average share of social wealth across reasonable scenarios.
context: Rawls argued the original position blocks the standard expected-utility calculation: with no probabilities to weight, the rational choice is the one whose worst possible result is least bad. The 'maximin' move is what gets the difference principle out of the veil — not risk aversion as a psychological quirk, but as the only rule that fits a choice made in genuine ignorance of one's own future.

question: Williams pictured Jim: a captain has lined up twenty villagers; shoot one and nineteen go free, refuse and all twenty die. Utilitarianism says shoot. Williams's objection was not about cruelty, rules, or virtue. What was it?
answer: Utilitarianism treats Jim as a neutral conduit for impersonal calculation, dissolving the projects and commitments that make him this agent.
choices: Utilitarianism treats Jim as a neutral conduit for impersonal calculation, dissolving the projects and commitments that make him this agent.
Utilitarianism wrongly counts the captain's cruelty as one more disutility, missing that killing innocents is a distinct wrong (Murdoch/Anscombe).
The arithmetic is correct, but the precedent erodes society's general inhibition against killing innocents — a rule-consequentialist worry.
Refusing expresses a compassion the captain lacks; virtue ethics judges by character rather than consequences, and commends refusal here.
context: Williams used the Jim case in 'A Critique of Utilitarianism' (1973) to show that utilitarian calculation cannot recognize the personal shape of moral life. Jim is not a neutral calculator; he is a particular person with projects and commitments that constitute who he is. Asking him to shoot — even when the arithmetic says shoot — alienates him from his own moral agency. The three rival objections (cruelty, rule-erosion, virtue-ethics reframing) are presented alongside as the standard contenders.

question: MacIntyre's After Virtue (1981): emotivism — 'X is good' means 'I approve, do as I do' — is wrong as theory of how moral language should work, yet accurate of how it now functions. How can both halves be true?
answer: Aristotle's framework — humans aimed at a telos at which virtues let us flourish — once gave 'good' real content. We lost it; the words remain, and now function emotively, as emotivism describes.
choices: Aristotle's framework — humans aimed at a telos at which virtues let us flourish — once gave 'good' real content. We lost it; the words remain, and now function emotively, as emotivism describes.
Moral language never had genuine cognitive content from the start; emotivists notice aloud what other ethical schools had long obscured behind layers of metaphysical apparatus and pretended depth.
Modern science showed there are no moral facts to refer to, so whatever teleology the older Aristotelian tradition imagined was false from the start (Mackie's error theory, no loss involved).
The institutions that trained moral judgment — church, guild, village — have collapsed; private morality necessarily becomes emotive once communal practice no longer anchors its day-to-day use.
context: In After Virtue (1981), MacIntyre argued that modern moral debates feel interminable because we use moral language detached from the Aristotelian framework — virtues directed at a human telos — that once made the language tractable. Emotivism is false as a theory of how moral language must work, but a correct description of how it works now. Distractor B is the strong emotivism MacIntyre rejects; C is a Mackie-flavored error-theory reading; D is a sociological gloss that misses MacIntyre's specifically Aristotelian point.

question: Anscombe argued in 1958 that modern secular ethics keeps using one word that no longer fits its framework. Which word, and why?
answer: 'Ought' — it presupposes a law and a lawgiver, but modern ethics rejected the divine framework that supplied both
choices: 'Ought' — it presupposes a law and a lawgiver, but modern ethics rejected the divine framework that supplied both
'Virtue' — it presupposes a fixed human nature, but modern ethics treats persons as self-defining beings without one
'Conscience' — it presupposes an inner voice from God, but modern ethics treats it as mere social conditioning
'Sin' — it presupposes guilt before a deity, but modern ethics retains it only as a metaphor for breaking rules
context: Anscombe's 'Modern Moral Philosophy' (1958) argued that the special moral 'ought' is a survival from a divine-law conception of ethics. Without a lawgiver, the concept is stranded — a feeling of force without the source that supplied it. Her recommendation was to drop the term until philosophy has an adequate psychology of action. The paper helped launch the twentieth-century virtue ethics revival, though Anscombe herself was a Catholic philosopher with a different motivation than later secular revivalists.

question: Suhrawardi, executed at 36 in Aleppo, founded Illuminationism. Aristotle's recipe for definition — broader kind (animal) plus distinguishing trait (rational) — works for ordinary things but fails on the deepest realities: light, pain, self. What did he offer?
answer: Direct presence. Light shines, pain hurts, the self is self-aware — known by their own appearance, not by placement under a wider genus. He called it luminous self-disclosure.
choices: Direct presence. Light shines, pain hurts, the self is self-aware — known by their own appearance, not by placement under a wider genus. He called it luminous self-disclosure.
Negation alone — for these realities we can only say what each is not (not finite, not dark, not divided); every positive statement we attempt falsifies the thing it tries to describe.
Mystical silence — the highest objects of thought are reached only when the philosopher gives up speech and reasoning; they cannot be theorized, only encountered in inward wordless attention.
Demonstration from cause — to know what light truly is, we must show what physical or metaphysical agency produces it; the philosopher's task is the patient business of causal explanation.
context: Shihab al-Din al-Suhrawardi's Hikmat al-Ishraq recast the Platonic Forms as degrees of light and grounded knowledge in unmediated self-presence rather than in Aristotelian syllogism. The tradition shaped Persian philosophy for centuries through Mulla Sadra. Suhrawardi was executed in Aleppo in 1191 on the orders of Saladin's son.

question: Two voices speak in practical reason. Egoism: pursue your own good. Utilitarianism: pursue the general good. Sidgwick spent The Methods of Ethics trying to show that on reflection these collapse into one principle. He could not. What did he call the gap?
answer: The 'dualism of practical reason' — both voices look self-evident on honest reflection, neither yields to the other, and reason alone cannot say which to obey when they pull apart.
choices: The 'dualism of practical reason' — both voices look self-evident on honest reflection, neither yields to the other, and reason alone cannot say which to obey when they pull apart.
The 'is-ought gap' — no description of what nature is can ever ground a prescription about how one ought to act, so ethics floats free of empirical fact and natural science alike.
The 'naturalistic fallacy' — 'good' cannot be defined by any natural property such as pleasure (Moore, 1903), so utilitarianism's identification of good with pleasure fails at the first step.
The 'fact-value distinction' — values are projected onto a neutral natural world, so two rational agents may genuinely disagree about values without either being in error about the world.
context: Sidgwick admitted at the close of his great book that without an appeal to theism — a moral order in which doing right and doing well coincide — practical reason fractured. Either pursue your own happiness or the general happiness; each looked self-evident, and reason alone could not arbitrate. He called this the most discouraging conclusion of his life's work.

question: Husserl took from Brentano the claim that every mental act reaches out toward an object — fear is fear of, hope is hope of. What did Husserl add to this picture of intentionality?
answer: Each act has a paired noesis (the meaning-act) and noema (object-as-meant) — the object's mode of givenness is itself part of the act.
choices: A real external cause behind each act, since without a worldly cause the apparent directedness of the mind would have no content to fix on at all.
A hidden drive expressed by each act, making the conscious object a mere screen onto which deeper unconscious aims project themselves systematically.
Each act has a paired noesis (the meaning-act) and noema (object-as-meant) — the object's mode of givenness is itself part of the act.
A neural process realizing each act, so 'aboutness' is finally a relation between brain states and the causal environment they have evolved to track.
context: Brentano in 1874 revived intentionality from the Scholastics. Husserl's Logical Investigations and Ideas I added the noesis/noema pair: the same tree can be perceived, doubted, remembered, or hoped-for; the aspect under which the object is given belongs to the act itself, not merely to a private inner image of the thing.

question: Husserl asked readers to suspend, not deny, the world's reality. He called this the epoché (bracketing). What did he say became visible only with the bracket in place?
answer: The structures of experience itself — how a tree is given as continuous, sided, mine to walk around — features hidden while we ask only whether it exists.
choices: The structures of experience itself — how a tree is given as continuous, sided, mine to walk around — features hidden while we ask only whether it exists.
The neural basis of perception, since stripping attention from the world lets the brain's own contribution to seeing become the proper topic of inquiry now.
The unconscious motives behind perception, since suspending the world lets long-repressed material rise into the bracketed field of consciousness here.
The cultural categories shaping perception, since bracketing reveals 'a tree' is a label our community has taught us to apply to a bundle of leaves and bark.
context: Greek epoché means suspension. This is not Cartesian doubt: Descartes asked whether the world is real and tried to answer. Husserl asks the existence question to be set aside, so perception's own structure — horizons, temporal flow, bodily anchoring — can come forward.

question: Writing as Europe slid toward war, Husserl named a crisis: science had grown so powerful it forgot the everyday lived world — the Lebenswelt. What was his specific charge?
answer: They had mistaken mathematized nature for nature itself — treating the measured world as more real than the lived world any measuring presupposes.
choices: They had mistaken mathematized nature for nature itself — treating the measured world as more real than the lived world any measuring presupposes.
They had served the rising totalitarian regimes, lending authority and prestige to states whose end was political domination rather than the pursuit of truth.
They had embraced positivism's verification rule, locking themselves out of any question — ethics, meaning, beauty — that no laboratory experiment could settle.
They had grown so overspecialized that disciplines could no longer talk across their boundaries to assemble a single coherent picture of the natural order.
context: Crisis of European Sciences (1936). Husserl saw Galileo's mathematization of nature as a brilliant move that had eaten its own foundation. The scientist measures with hands, eyes, instruments, in a workshop, in a culture — features of the Lebenswelt. Treating the equations as the real and the lived world as illusion forgets what made the equations possible.

question: Heidegger refused to call us 'rational animals' or 'subjects.' He used Dasein — 'being-there' — to mark what older labels missed. What structural feature sets Dasein apart, on his account?
answer: Dasein is the being for whom its own being is an issue — it cares what it is, projects possibilities, and must take a stance on its existence.
choices: Dasein is the being equipped with reason and language, able to grasp universal essences that other animals can only respond to as bare biological stimuli.
Dasein is the being made in the image of God, bearing a rational soul whose dignity grounds the rights that distinguish persons from mere things in nature.
Dasein is the being for whom its own being is an issue — it cares what it is, projects possibilities, and must take a stance on its existence.
Dasein is the being shaped by social structures — kinship, language, economy — that no animal inherits and that determine what each individual can come to be.
context: Being and Time (1927). Heidegger chose Dasein to avoid every loaded inheritance: not soul, not mind, not subject, not consciousness. The hyphen in being-there marks what he wanted in view: a being whose being is in question for it. The rock does not care whether it is a rock; Dasein cares whether it is itself.

question: Heidegger gave long sections of Being and Time to being-toward-death — facing one's finite end. He insisted this was not a meditation on mortality as biological event. What existential structure was he after?
answer: Death as my ownmost possibility — the one no one can take over for me; owning rather than fleeing it lets me live my own life, not the anonymous one.
choices: Death as the gateway to the soul's true homeland — the religious horizon against which earthly attachments shrink and the order of goods is at last restored.
Death as the great equalizer — the biological fact that rich and poor alike must die, which dissolves the vanities of rank and grounds the demand to be just.
Death as a natural process to be accepted — the Stoic discipline of consenting to what nature requires, freeing the mind from futile fear of a sure terminus.
Death as my ownmost possibility — the one no one can take over for me; owning rather than fleeing it lets me live my own life, not the anonymous one.
context: Being and Time §§46–53. The point is not 'we all die, so be serious.' Death is the one possibility no one can take over for me. Recognizing this strips away the everyday flight into how 'one' lives, what 'one' does. Authentic existence is not gloomy heroism — it is owning the finitude that makes any particular life mine.

question: Heidegger pictured picking up a hammer. As the work flows, the hammer vanishes into the task — ready-to-hand. When the head flies off, it stares back as a thing — present-at-hand. What broader claim did he draw?
answer: Things show up first as equipment inside practical involvements, not as neutral objects with properties — the workshop is more basic than the laboratory.
choices: Tool-use is the evolutionary origin of cognition, so studying how early primates handled sticks reveals a structure shared by every later human thought.
Things show up first as equipment inside practical involvements, not as neutral objects with properties — the workshop is more basic than the laboratory.
Practical know-how is inferior to theoretical knowledge — only when the hammer breaks and is contemplated does the object become available to philosophy.
Objects exist only as bundles of perceptions in an observer's mind — the broken hammer reveals the constructed nature of the world its user had been assuming.
context: Being and Time §§15–18. The hammer example overturns a long default: the world as substances with properties (Descartes, Locke). Heidegger says that's a breakdown picture. Primary access is engaged — hammer for-hammering, nail for-fastening, wall for-sheltering. Theoretical staring is what happens when the practical world snags, not what underlies it.

question: Heidegger said every Dasein finds itself underway — born into a body, language, century, mood — none chosen. He called this thrownness (Geworfenheit). What did the term add?
answer: Facticity is not contingent backdrop but the structure of existence — Dasein never starts from a neutral zero; it is always already partway through a situation.
choices: Circumstance determines character — choices are products of environment, and the appearance of freedom reduces to ignorance about the real causes at work.
Facticity is not contingent backdrop but the structure of existence — Dasein never starts from a neutral zero; it is always already partway through a situation.
Suffering is universal and instructive — the unchosen conditions teach humility and form a moral education that an easier life would have spared us from having.
Society shapes the self at every level — any account of personal freedom that ignores class, race, and gender is naive about the conditions that make agency possible.
context: Being and Time §29. Geworfenheit names a structural feature, not a sad fact. Sartre would later say existence precedes essence; for Heidegger no Dasein ever stands at a Sartrean zero point. The situation is already begun, the mood is already set, the possibilities are already narrowed. Projection always rides on thrownness.

question: Merleau-Ponty said Descartes left a riddle: a mind that thinks, a body that moves, no account of how they meet. He dissolved it by denying the body is a thing the self owns. What was his move?
answer: The body is itself the subject — perception, motion, and meaning live in its skilled engagement with the world, not in an inner consciousness inspecting it.
choices: The body is a refined machine and the soul a real immaterial substance, so their meeting happens in some organ that future science will eventually locate.
The body is itself the subject — perception, motion, and meaning live in its skilled engagement with the world, not in an inner consciousness inspecting it.
The mind is identical with brain processes — the apparent gap is a confusion of vocabularies; neuroscience will translate every mental term into a physical one.
Behavior is the whole story — talk of inner mental states adds nothing to the publicly observable movements a rigorous scientific psychology can describe.
context: Phenomenology of Perception (1945). Merleau-Ponty rejected both halves of Cartesian dualism without retreating to materialism. The body reaching for a cup already knows where the cup is; the hand learning to type already grasps the keyboard's shape. Subjectivity is not behind the body looking out — it lives in the body's perceptual-motor dialogue with a world.

question: Medieval thinkers fought over whether universals like 'redness' or 'humanity' exist. Abelard rejected both pure realism and pure nominalism. What was his middle path?
answer: Universals are not things but mental concepts (sermones) abstracted from real similarities among particulars.
choices: Universals are not things but mental concepts (sermones) abstracted from real similarities among particulars.
Universals are real things existing apart from particulars, accessed by intellect as Plato's Forms taught.
Universals are real things in particulars themselves, the shared form embedded in each member of a kind.
Universals are merely names (flatus vocis) — breath in the air with no foundation in things at all.
context: Abelard's *Logica Ingredientibus* threads between Roscelin's pure nominalism (universals are just sounds) and William of Champeaux's pure realism (universals are things). His conceptualism: the mind abstracts a common concept from real resemblances — neither inventing the likeness nor finding a Platonic Form. The position resurfaces in Locke, Hume, and contemporary 'trope theory' debates.

question: Duns Scotus asked what makes Socrates *this* Socrates rather than merely an instance of humanity. His answer added a new metaphysical layer. What did he call it?
answer: Haecceitas — a thing's individual 'thisness,' a positive principle distinguishing each from every other.
choices: Haecceitas — a thing's individual 'thisness,' a positive principle distinguishing each from every other.
Quidditas — a thing's 'whatness,' the shared essence that makes it the kind of thing it ultimately is.
Materia signata — matter marked by quantity, the Thomist principle that one human differs from another.
Hypokeimenon — Aristotle's underlying substrate, the bare particular bearing all properties of a thing.
context: Scotus rejected Aquinas's view that individuation comes from 'signate matter' (matter with specific dimensions) — that would make pure spirits like angels indistinguishable. His alternative: each individual has a haecceity, a primitive principle of thisness, irreducible to any form, matter, or accident. Gerard Manley Hopkins, the Victorian poet, called it 'inscape' and credited Scotus with showing him how to see particulars as unrepeatable.

question: Does 'exists' mean the same in 'God exists' and 'this oak exists'? Aquinas said no — it applies analogically (by likeness, not same sense). Scotus: it applies univocally — same sense — to both. What was his argument?
answer: If 'being' meant something different of God than of creatures, we could not form the thought 'God exists' — minds would lack a shared concept to extend. One minimum concept must apply the same way.
choices: If 'being' meant something different of God than of creatures, we could not form the thought 'God exists' — minds would lack a shared concept to extend. One minimum concept must apply the same way.
Being is predicated of God and creatures equivocally — they share only the bare noise of 'exists,' with no real concept the human mind can hold in common between the two cases at all.
Being is predicated of God only negatively — we can say what God is not (not finite, not temporal, not material), never anything positive, since finite minds cannot grasp the infinite directly.
Being is grasped only by direct mystical vision — what 'exists' means when said of God is encountered, never conceived; theology only records the vision rather than reasoning to it from premises.
context: Scotus's argument: if 'being' shifted meaning between God and creatures, we could not even *form* the thought 'God exists' — our minds would have no shared concept to extend. So one minimum-content concept of being must apply univocally; analogy enters only at the level of *how* a being is, not *that* it is. The dispute shaped Christian philosophy for centuries; Heidegger blamed univocity for inaugurating the 'forgetting of being.'

question: Aquinas treated intellect as ruling will; the intellect sees the good and the will follows. Duns Scotus reversed the order. What did he claim about the relation?
answer: The will is free to choose against what intellect judges best; freedom is the will's primacy, not its servitude.
choices: The will is free to choose against what intellect judges best; freedom is the will's primacy, not its servitude.
The will is the executor only; if intellect judges rightly, the will must follow what reason has clearly seen.
The will is moved by passion alone; reason is the slave of the passions, as Hume would later restate it.
The will is determined entirely by grace; without supernatural aid, the will cannot move toward the good.
context: Scotus's voluntarism: the will is the noblest faculty because it alone is genuinely free. Intellect cannot but assent to what is clearly true (you cannot decide 2+2=5); only the will can choose between alternatives both presented as good. The position pushes back against Aquinas's intellectualism and prepares the ground for modern accounts of liberty. Critics worry it threatens to make God's will arbitrary; defenders say it grounds real moral responsibility.

question: Frege distinguished sense (Sinn) from reference (Bedeutung). "The morning star" and "the evening star" both refer to Venus — yet he denied they mean the same thing. Why does the difference matter?
answer: Without it, "morning star = evening star" would be as trivial as "Venus = Venus" — yet it was a real astronomical discovery
choices: Without it, "morning star = evening star" would be as trivial as "Venus = Venus" — yet it was a real astronomical discovery
Reference fixes truth, but each speaker means a private image by the phrase, so the names belong to two distinct mental languages
The phrases pick out Venus only in scientific contexts; in ordinary speech they refer to whatever bright body the sky happens to show
Names without descriptive content cannot substitute in belief reports, so each must secretly encode a hidden definite description
context: Frege's 1892 essay "Über Sinn und Bedeutung." Reference is what a term picks out in the world; sense is the "mode of presentation" — the route by which the term reaches its referent. Identity claims a=b are informative when a and b have different senses but the same reference. This single distinction underwrites most of 20th-century philosophy of language.

question: What is a number? Frege's 1884 Grundlagen answered logically. Take five: fingers on a hand, points on a star, the Great Lakes. What such collections share, he said, is being 'equinumerous' — same size. So 5 is the set of concepts equinumerous with 'finger on a hand.' The hidden claim?
answer: Numbers are objects of pure logic — not of the mind, not of physical groups. If number is defined by equinumerosity (a logical relation), arithmetic is logic in disguise.
choices: Numbers are objects of pure logic — not of the mind, not of physical groups. If number is defined by equinumerosity (a logical relation), arithmetic is logic in disguise.
Numbers are mental constructions the mind forms by abstracting away the differences between groups and retaining only their bare quantitative likeness (the psychologist's view).
Numbers are linguistic conventions — convenient labels for tracking collections, with no existence outside the social practices of speakers using the labels in everyday counting.
Numbers are properties of physical aggregates of objects, so 'three' picks out a feature shared by every real-world collection containing exactly three items (Mill's empiricist proposal).
context: Frege's logicist program. He attacked Mill (numbers as features of physical aggregates), Kant (numbers as synthetic a priori intuitions of time), and the psychologists (numbers as mental images). His alternative: number-statements are claims about *concepts*, and concepts plus equinumerosity belong to logic alone. The program collapsed when Russell sent his paradox in 1902 — but the question of what numbers are has never recovered.

question: Russell's 1905 "On Denoting" tackled "The present King of France is bald." There is no king of France — so true, false, or meaningless? His move dissolved the puzzle. What did he do?
answer: Rewrote it as three logical claims: there is a king of France, there is only one, and he is bald — so the whole sentence is simply false
choices: Rewrote it as three logical claims: there is a king of France, there is only one, and he is bald — so the whole sentence is simply false
Argued the phrase refers to a non-existent object that subsists in a separate realm of being, making the sentence meaningful and false
Treated the description as a disguised proper name whose meaning is fixed by a cluster of features speakers tie to French monarchy
Held that the sentence lacks any truth value because its subject term fails to refer — a case of presupposition failure, not falsity
context: Russell's theory of definite descriptions. "The F is G" gets analyzed as "there exists exactly one F, and it is G." His real target was Meinong, who populated reality with non-existent objects to keep such sentences meaningful. Russell showed the puzzle was an illusion of surface grammar — *logical form* hides quantifiers the grammar disguises. Strawson later attacked with the presupposition-failure view (choice 4), making this an enduring dispute.

question: In 1902 Russell sent Frege a letter that destroyed his life work. Consider the set of all sets not members of themselves. Is it a member of itself? Either answer contradicts the other. What did the paradox show?
answer: Frege's axiom that every concept defines a set was inconsistent — you cannot let any well-formed condition carve out a set without breeding contradictions
choices: Frege's axiom that every concept defines a set was inconsistent — you cannot let any well-formed condition carve out a set without breeding contradictions
Mathematics could not be founded on set theory at all, since collections of abstract objects turned out to be a fundamentally incoherent notion
Self-reference is illegitimate in any formal system, so axioms must explicitly forbid any sentence that mentions the system it belongs to
Infinite collections cannot be treated as completed totalities, leaving only finite sets as legitimate mathematical objects for foundations
context: Russell's paradox, 1902. Frege had just sent volume 2 of the Grundgesetze to press; in the appendix he wrote that "a scientist can hardly meet with anything more undesirable than to have the foundation give way as the work is finished." His fix didn't hold. Russell's eventual escape was type theory — stratifying objects into levels so the paradoxical set couldn't even be formed. Zermelo's separation axiom became the standard repair instead.

question: Russell's escape from his own paradox was the theory of types. Sets sort into a hierarchy: individuals at level 0, sets of individuals at level 1, sets of those at level 2. Why does stratification block the paradox?
answer: "The set of all sets not members of themselves" cannot even be formed — a level-n set may only contain level-(n−1) things, so self-membership is ungrammatical
choices: "The set of all sets not members of themselves" cannot even be formed — a level-n set may only contain level-(n−1) things, so self-membership is ungrammatical
Each level has its own logical rules, so contradictions detected at one level fail to propagate downward and threaten lower-level consistency
Higher-level sets are fictions introduced for convenience, and fictions cannot generate genuine contradictions about anything actually real
The hierarchy is finite in practice, so paradox-generating sets lie beyond any level mathematicians actually use and pose no working danger
context: Principia Mathematica's ramified type theory. The cost was steep: types had to be repeated, an "axiom of reducibility" smuggled assumptions back in, and the whole edifice became baroque. Later set theorists preferred Zermelo-Fraenkel's looser separation axiom. But the typing idea survived: it is the ancestor of every modern type system in programming languages, from ML to Haskell to Rust.

question: Principia Mathematica ran three volumes; it took until page 379 of volume 1 to prove 1+1=2. Russell and Whitehead weren't being slow. What were they trying to do that required such patience?
answer: Derive every arithmetical truth from purely logical axioms with no mathematical assumption smuggled in — every move had to be justified before arithmetic could appear
choices: Derive every arithmetical truth from purely logical axioms with no mathematical assumption smuggled in — every move had to be justified before arithmetic could appear
Build a notation general enough to express every theorem ever proven, so the early volumes were spent designing the symbolic apparatus itself
Catalogue every known proof of basic arithmetic into one system, exposing redundancies in mathematical practice that nineteenth-century rigor missed
Replace ordinary mathematics with a constructive alternative in which only objects explicitly buildable from prior objects would be allowed in proofs
context: Principia Mathematica (1910–1913). The logicist project: arithmetic is logic in disguise. They never finished — volume 4, on geometry, was abandoned. The famous page-379 proof of "1+1=2" carries a wry footnote: "The above proposition is occasionally useful." Gödel's 1931 incompleteness theorems would later show the larger project couldn't succeed in principle, but the technical apparatus reshaped logic permanently.

question: G.E. Moore raised his hand at a 1939 lecture: "Here is one hand." Then the other: "And here is another." He claimed this refuted skepticism about the external world. Why did this work?
answer: He was more certain his hands existed than of any premise leading to skepticism — so the skeptical argument must contain a less certain premise to reject
choices: He was more certain his hands existed than of any premise leading to skepticism — so the skeptical argument must contain a less certain premise to reject
Direct sense perception is logically prior to philosophical reasoning, so any conclusion conflicting with what we see is refuted by the perceptual evidence
Skeptics depend on language shared with non-skeptics, so denying that hands exist already presupposes the common-sense framework they wished to deny
Holding up a hand is a public act witnesses can verify, so the existence of the hand is confirmed independently by everyone present at the demonstration
context: Moore's 1939 "Proof of an External World." The move looks naive but is sophisticated: Moore wasn't claiming to refute the skeptic on the skeptic's own terms. He was running the argument backward — if a chain of reasoning leads to "no hands exist," but I am more sure hands exist than of any link in the chain, I am rationally entitled to reject the chain. Wittgenstein took the move seriously enough to spend his last notebook (On Certainty) wrestling with it.

question: Frege made a sentence that looks like a joke: "the concept horse is not a concept." His point: in "Bessie is a horse," the words "is a horse" don't name a thing — they say something of Bessie. He called that role predicative. What goes wrong if you try to refer to a concept by saying "the concept horse"?
answer: The phrase puts the concept into a name-slot, but concepts live in the predicate-slot ("…is a horse"). Naming one converts it into an object — the kind of thing concepts apply to.
choices: The phrase puts the concept into a name-slot, but concepts live in the predicate-slot ("…is a horse"). Naming one converts it into an object — the kind of thing concepts apply to.
Concepts are private mental items, so language can only point at them indirectly, through the public objects different thinkers happen to share between them.
Universals like horseness lack independent existence, so phrases that look like they name a universal must really be naming some class of similar individuals.
Names refer through descriptions, and concepts lack descriptions, so "the concept horse" must denote whichever description fits the predicative role.
context: Frege's 1892 "On Concept and Object." In "the horse is brown," "the horse" is the object slot, "is brown" is the concept slot. The two roles cannot exchange. The paradox: no theory of the distinction can be stated without violating it. Wittgenstein turned this into the Tractarian doctrine of what can be shown but not said.

question: Fichte built his system on one act: the self wakes up by positing itself — saying, in effect, "I am." Call that bare self the I. But Fichte said a pure I, with nothing standing against it, would be empty — nothing for it to be aware of, not even itself. So self-positing alone is not enough. What else must the I do?
answer: Posit a not-I — something other than itself, standing against it as a limit. Only by bumping into what it is not does the I become aware of being an I at all.
choices: Posit a not-I — something other than itself, standing against it as a limit. Only by bumping into what it is not does the I become aware of being an I at all.
Posit a divine ground beyond itself; without an infinite anchor, the finite act of self-positing simply collapses into illusion, and the I dissolves back into nothing.
Posit impressions arriving from outside; experience is given to the I by the world, and the I is only ever what reflects back what is given to it from outside.
Posit a fixed essence inside itself; the conscious life flows out of a soul or substance that quietly grounds the unity of the mind before any act of thought.
context: Fichte's Wissenschaftslehre begins with the self-positing act of the I. A pure I, with nothing facing it, is empty. The I must posit a not-I; only against that limit does it know itself as the active subject it is.

question: Hegel never wrote the formula thesis-antithesis-synthesis in his major works; the triad came from a Fichte summary. What is his real move?
answer: A concept pressed strictly contains its own opposite; the contradiction is lifted into a richer concept holding both.
choices: A concept pressed strictly contains its own opposite; the contradiction is lifted into a richer concept holding both.
A thesis is set against an antithesis; reason picks whichever side has the stronger empirical evidence behind it.
A claim is tested by deducing consequences; if they fail, the claim is replaced by a wholly new claim built fresh.
A position is asserted as truth; opposing claims are refuted by common sense and the tradition's broad consensus.
context: The textbook triad is a Chalybaus summary of Fichte that stuck to Hegel by accident. Hegel's actual move is immanent: follow a concept far enough and it turns into its opposite. The new concept (Aufhebung) cancels, preserves, and lifts the prior pair.

question: Hegel's word Geist gets translated as Spirit or Mind, but neither quite fits. What does Geist actually name in his use?
answer: A shared life of self-aware reason carried by persons and institutions, growing toward fuller self-knowledge.
choices: A shared life of self-aware reason carried by persons and institutions, growing toward fuller self-knowledge.
A divine personal substance distinct from the world, acting on history from outside as providence directs it.
A psychological faculty inside each individual; the private inner stream of thought conscious beings share.
A material force underlying nature; the productive energy that completed physics will eventually describe.
context: Geist is not a ghost, not a private psyche, not a force of nature. It is reason as a shared, public life carried in laws, art, religion, and philosophy. History, for Hegel, is Geist coming to recognize itself in what it has built.

question: Kojeve and Fukuyama drew the end of history thesis from Hegel. What did Hegel himself mean by saying history reaches an end?
answer: Not that events stop, but that the principle of freedom is achieved in principle, leaving only its working-out.
choices: Not that events stop, but that the principle of freedom is achieved in principle, leaving only its working-out.
That a final empire will unify all peoples under one rational state, ending political diversity for good.
That events become cyclical once reason matures; civilizations rise and fall on a pattern with no progress.
That philosophy itself ends with his system; later thinkers can only repeat what he has already shown them.
context: Kojeve read Hegel as predicting a final universal state; Fukuyama applied the line to 1989. Hegel's own claim was about a principle, not a date: once it is grasped that every person is free, the basic logic of history is complete. The working-out continues.

question: Schelling around 1801 offered a striking image: a single root beneath both the tree of thought and the tree of nature — one reality showing itself in two ways. He called this root the absolute, and the position identity philosophy. What was his core claim about that root?
answer: The root is not a finished thing but a productive activity — the same self-grounding power that produces nature also produces mind, and only its products show up as the two-sided world.
choices: The root is not a finished thing but a productive activity — the same self-grounding power that produces nature also produces mind, and only its products show up as the two-sided world.
The absolute is a perfect God beyond all finite things; mind and nature are created products that lie outside it and depend entirely on it for their being and order.
The absolute is the moral law within rational wills; mind and nature only matter as the field on which that commanding moral form takes effect in the world of action.
The absolute is bare matter in motion; mind is a late surface effect produced by the deeper physical processes that nature has quietly been running all along.
