choices: The slave — by working on the world, the slave shapes objects and comes to recognize his own activity, while the idle master stagnates.
The master — by winning the recognition stakes, the master gains the freedom to develop the higher capacities of mind without distraction.
Neither — the encounter is a dead end, and Hegel uses it to argue that real self-knowledge requires withdrawing from any social conflict.
Both equally — through their conflict, master and slave together develop the political institutions of the modern constitutional state.
context: Phenomenology of Spirit (1807). Marx read this as the kernel of his theory of labor; Kojève's 1930s Paris lectures shaped a generation of French thought.

question: Schelling broke with Fichte around 1800. Fichte built everything on the I — nature, for Fichte, was a stage set the I posits to have something to overcome. Schelling refused this asymmetry. What did his Naturphilosophie claim instead?
answer: Nature is not dead matter posited by mind but a living, productive activity — mind and nature are one absolute seen from two sides.
choices: Nature is not dead matter posited by mind but a living, productive activity — mind and nature are one absolute seen from two sides.
Nature is a mechanical clockwork created by God at the start, with mind being a thinking substance entirely independent of its workings.
Nature is a system of forces explained completely by Newtonian physics, and philosophy should restrict itself to the mental side of reality.
Nature is an illusion projected by the transcendental ego, and the goal of philosophy is to dissolve it into a finally clear self-knowledge.
context: Ideas for a Philosophy of Nature (1797). His identity philosophy followed: the absolute is the indifference point of mind and nature.

question: Hegel's word Geist gets translated as Spirit, Mind, sometimes Ghost. None is quite right. Kojève and the French read it one way; the British idealists another. What is closer to what Geist actually names across the Phenomenology?
answer: The shared life of a people — customs, language, law, art, religion — a collective subject that thinks through its individual members.
choices: The shared life of a people — customs, language, law, art, religion — a collective subject that thinks through its individual members.
An individual immortal soul that survives the death of the body and reunites with God in a personal afterlife awaiting it after history.
A nonmaterial substance pervading the universe that explains apparent supernatural phenomena like apparitions and inspired prophecy.
A psychological faculty distinguishing humans from animals, located by Hegel in the cerebral cortex and studied through introspection.
context: Hegel speaks of objective Geist (institutions, customs) and absolute Geist (art, religion, philosophy) as stages of one developing reality.

question: Fichte's Wissenschaftslehre starts not from God, not from substance, not from sense data, but from one self-positing act. The I says 'I am' — that bare saying is the bedrock. Why did Fichte think every other starting point smuggles assumptions?
answer: Any object you start from has already been presented to consciousness — so consciousness is logically prior to anything posited as outside it.
choices: Any object you start from has already been presented to consciousness — so consciousness is logically prior to anything posited as outside it.
Sense data are unreliable because the senses can be deceived; only mathematical truths supply a starting point firm enough to build on.
God's existence cannot be proved, so a system grounded in theology builds on a hypothesis no later step can fully justify or warrant.
Substance is plural and contested; ancient atomists and Cartesians disagreed about it, so no starting point in metaphysics is neutral.
context: Foundations of the Entire Wissenschaftslehre (1794). Fichte radicalized Kant's transcendental I; Schelling and Hegel each broke with him later.

question: Kant had put a wall between us and the thing-in-itself: we see only appearances, never the world as it is. Schopenhauer agreed the wall was real for almost everything — but said each of us already stands on the other side at one point. Where?
answer: Your own willing — felt from the inside as desire and effort, it is the thing-in-itself as you happen to know it directly in one single case.
choices: Your own willing — felt from the inside as desire and effort, it is the thing-in-itself as you happen to know it directly in one single case.
Your own perceiving — careful introspection on sensory experience reveals the structure underlying the appearances that Kant left mysterious.
Your own reasoning — pure logical deduction lets you step outside appearance entirely and grasp the necessary structure of reality.
Your own dreaming — under sleep conscious filtering relaxes and the mind contacts deeper layers of reality otherwise hidden behind it.
context: The World as Will and Representation (1819). Every plant, animal, and stone is the same striving Will under different appearances.

question: Sartre describes peering through a keyhole, absorbed in what he sees — then he hears footsteps in the hall. Suddenly he feels seen. Shame floods him. Sartre used the scene in Being and Nothingness to make a philosophical point about other people. What was it?
answer: Another person's gaze reveals me to myself as an object in their world — I encounter my own being-for-others, and shame is its mark.
choices: Another person's gaze reveals me to myself as an object in their world — I encounter my own being-for-others, and shame is its mark.
Privacy is a basic moral right grounded in human dignity, and political theory must build its institutions to defend that right above all.
Bodies are governed by social conventions about respectable conduct, and most behaviors a person calls private are quietly regulated by class.
Conscience is the internalized voice of the parents and society, and its judgments simply repeat what the larger group has already decided.
context: Being and Nothingness, Part III. Sartre's account of the Look is one of the most cited passages in 20th-century philosophy.

question: Sartre's most famous example of bad faith is the Paris café waiter — too precise, too solicitous, gliding from table to table performing the role with theatrical exactness. Sartre is not mocking him. What is the philosophical point about what the waiter is doing?
answer: He is trying to become his social role through and through, denying his freedom to step out of it — bad faith is fleeing freedom into a fixed identity.
choices: He is trying to become his social role through and through, denying his freedom to step out of it — bad faith is fleeing freedom into a fixed identity.
He is performing for tips with calculated insincerity, and bad faith is simply the older name for the kind of lying every service economy requires.
He is suffering class oppression that makes the role unavoidable, and Sartre frames bad faith as a problem economic reorganization would solve.
He is dissociated from his bodily presence through long working hours, and bad faith names the resulting alienation from his physical self.
context: Being and Nothingness, Part I, ch. 2. Sartre's point: the waiter is free even now to refuse the role; pretending he simply IS a waiter is the lie.

question: Albert Camus opened The Myth of Sisyphus (1942) with one startling sentence: 'There is but one truly serious philosophical problem, and that is suicide.' He spent the book working out his answer — neither suicide nor what he called the 'philosophical suicide' of religion. What is the third option?
answer: Revolt — to keep facing the absurd contradiction between human longing for meaning and the world's silence, without giving up on either side.
choices: Revolt — to keep facing the absurd contradiction between human longing for meaning and the world's silence, without giving up on either side.
Surrender — to abandon the demand for meaning, accept that the question itself is malformed, and live as untroubled animals seem to live.
Distraction — to fill every waking hour with work, family, and small pleasures so that the larger question never has the room to surface.
Faith — to commit to a religious tradition despite knowing it cannot be rationally established, on the grounds that some commitment is better than none.
context: The Myth of Sisyphus (1942) ends: 'One must imagine Sisyphus happy.' The boulder always rolls back; he keeps pushing.

question: Husserl's epoché — bracketing — asks the philosopher to suspend the natural attitude, the unexamined assumption that the world is independently there. He insisted this was not skepticism. He was not doubting the world. What was he doing?
answer: Setting aside the question of the world's independent existence in order to describe carefully how it shows up in consciousness in the first place.
choices: Setting aside the question of the world's independent existence in order to describe carefully how it shows up in consciousness in the first place.
Arguing that the world does not exist outside the mind, and that all objects of perception are mental constructs without external reference.
Denying that science can know anything about the world, and recommending a return to ordinary commonsense reports of perception.
Replacing logic with intuition as the criterion of truth, on the grounds that careful introspection reveals certainties that proof cannot.
context: Ideas I (1913). Bracketing lets phenomenology study how experience is structured (intentional acts and their objects) without metaphysical claims.

question: Frege's 1884 Grundlagen der Arithmetik attacked the picture of numbers as marks on paper, mental ideas in heads, or piles of objects in the world. He insisted numbers are none of those. What did Frege argue a number is?
answer: An objective abstract object that attaches to a concept — 'the number 7' belongs to the concept 'days of the week,' not to any particular collection of items.
choices: An objective abstract object that attaches to a concept — 'the number 7' belongs to the concept 'days of the week,' not to any particular collection of items.
A mental image arising in the head of any human capable of counting — different humans share similar images, but each is private to its own bearer.
A linguistic convention that varies across languages — the apparent objectivity of arithmetic dissolves once we compare how cultures actually count.
A physical inscription that exists on a page or screen — without the marks, the number itself has no existence in the world of natural objects we know.
context: Die Grundlagen der Arithmetik (1884). Frege's anti-psychologism — numbers are objective, not psychological — set the agenda for analytic philosophy.

question: Russell's 1902 letter to Frege described a single set. Consider the set of all sets that are not members of themselves. Is that set a member of itself? Either answer breaks. Frege was finishing Volume II of Grundgesetze. What did the paradox show about his project?
answer: His basic law allowing any property to define a set led directly to contradiction — set theory needed a restriction Frege had not seen.
choices: His basic law allowing any property to define a set led directly to contradiction — set theory needed a restriction Frege had not seen.
His treatment of natural numbers as objects was incoherent because numbers really name properties of concepts, not things in their own right.
His distinction between sense and reference applied only to proper names and not to predicates, so the whole semantic theory needed redoing.
His system was sound but used a notation so awkward that mathematicians never adopted it and his results passed unnoticed for decades.
context: Frege added a hasty appendix and abandoned the project's logicist ambitions. Russell's later theory of types tried to patch the gap.

question: Russell's 1905 'On Denoting' tackled 'The present King of France is bald.' There is no king of France, so the sentence cannot be true. But 'The King of France is not bald' looks no better. Russell rewrote the surface form. What did he say the sentence really claims?
answer: Three claims at once: there is a king of France; there is at most one; and that one is bald — the first claim's failure is what makes the whole sentence false.
choices: Three claims at once: there is a king of France; there is at most one; and that one is bald — the first claim's failure is what makes the whole sentence false.
A single claim about a nonexistent object, which Russell took to refer to a special class of 'subsisting' beings populating a shadow ontology of their own.
An indexical claim whose meaning shifts with each speaker's context, requiring a richer logic of time and place than Frege's earlier system supplied.
A poetic claim governed by literary conventions rather than the rules of literal language, and so outside the proper domain of logic entirely as analyzed.
context: Russell's theory of descriptions — a paradigm of analytic method, dissolving a puzzle by paraphrasing surface form into logical form.

question: The early Wittgenstein in the 1921 Tractatus ended with a famous instruction: 'Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent.' The Vienna Circle read this as a clean ban on metaphysics. Wittgenstein wrote to a friend that the real point was the opposite. What did he mean?
answer: Everything important — ethics, value, the meaning of life — falls outside what language can say; it shows itself, and silence honors it.
choices: Everything important — ethics, value, the meaning of life — falls outside what language can say; it shows itself, and silence honors it.
Religion and ethics should be replaced by a public conversation of citizens about shared interests, with private faith confined to private life.
Mathematics and logic are nonsense in disguise; the apparent power of these subjects comes from their being unstated background assumptions.
Philosophy is dispensable once the natural sciences mature, and the silence is a long quiet that science will eventually deliver to thought.
context: Wittgenstein to Ludwig von Ficker, 1919. The Vienna Circle thought him dismissing the unsayable as nonsense; for him it was the important nonsense.

question: The early Wittgenstein claimed sentences 'picture' facts — they share a logical form with what they depict. By the 1930s he had broken with this entirely. Philosophical Investigations rejects the picture theory. What does Wittgenstein now say words get their meaning from?
answer: The rule-governed practices of using them — the 'language games' built into ordinary life, where meaning is use rather than picture.
choices: The rule-governed practices of using them — the 'language games' built into ordinary life, where meaning is use rather than picture.
Mental images that accompany them — to understand a word is to call up the right inner picture and check the world against it.
Definitions found in dictionaries — every word has a precise meaning given by an explicit rule fixed by linguistic experts.
The intentions of the speaker — what a word means in a sentence is whatever the speaker had in mind when using it at that moment.
context: Philosophical Investigations §§1–43. Chess pieces, building blocks, slabs — all examples of meaning grounded in use.

question: Carnap in a famous 1932 essay analyzed Heidegger's line 'the nothing itself noths' (das Nichts selbst nichtet). He did not call it false. He used it to illustrate a sharper charge against a class of metaphysical sentences. What was Carnap's charge?
answer: Such sentences are not false but cognitively meaningless — they violate the rules of logical syntax and so say nothing that could in principle be true or false.
choices: Such sentences are not false but cognitively meaningless — they violate the rules of logical syntax and so say nothing that could in principle be true or false.
Such sentences are politically dangerous because they prepare the ground for irrationalism — the same line of attack that would have stopped fascism in time.
Such sentences are merely poetic and belong in a separate domain — Heidegger had simply confused poetry with science by writing in apparent assertions.
Such sentences are correct but unprovable — they describe genuine features of being that lie outside what the verification principle is able to capture.
context: 'The Elimination of Metaphysics through Logical Analysis of Language' (1932). Carnap's reading helped harden the split between analytic and continental philosophy for decades.

question: Adorno and Horkheimer wrote Dialectic of Enlightenment (1944) in Los Angeles, refugees from the Nazis. The book's central claim is darker than any earlier Marxist line. The Enlightenment had promised emancipation through reason. What did they argue had instead happened?
answer: Instrumental reason had become a new form of domination — reducing humans and nature alike to means, and clearing the way for the camps.
choices: Instrumental reason had become a new form of domination — reducing humans and nature alike to means, and clearing the way for the camps.
Capitalist owners had captured the press and propagandized workers out of class consciousness, so revolution had become structurally impossible.
Religion's collapse left no moral framework, and so totalitarianism filled the vacuum left by churches that earlier centuries had relied on.
Mass democracy unleashed irrational majorities, and the educated elite had failed to defend constitutional limits when the test came.
context: Dialectic of Enlightenment (1944). The pessimism marked a break with classical Marxism, which had still seen rational progress as on the workers' side.

question: Foucault rejected the picture of power as something the strong own and use to repress the weak. The formula from History of Sexuality v.1 reverses this. Power, Foucault argued, is not mostly a force that says 'no.' What did he say it is?
answer: A productive network running through every relation — it shapes desires, identities, and knowledge rather than only blocking them from outside.
choices: A productive network running through every relation — it shapes desires, identities, and knowledge rather than only blocking them from outside.
A possession held by ruling classes — what changes through history is who holds it, not what it is or how it operates on those below.
An ideology spread through schools and media — power is essentially a set of beliefs the dominant class persuades subordinates to accept.
A monopoly of violence exercised by the state — wherever the legal use of force ends, the work of power ends with it for ordinary citizens.
context: History of Sexuality v.1 (1976). Foucault meant the move as method — analyze power as a circulating relation, not a thing the powerful own.

question: Foucault introduced 'biopolitics' to name a shift that began, on his account, around the late 18th century. Earlier sovereigns held the right to take life or let live — the king could kill, and otherwise stood back. Modern states work along a different axis. What is the new axis?
answer: Managing the life of populations — birthrates, public health, longevity, sexuality — through statistics, hygiene, and the welfare apparatus.
choices: Managing the life of populations — birthrates, public health, longevity, sexuality — through statistics, hygiene, and the welfare apparatus.
Monopolizing armed force inside national borders — modern states differ from older ones in finally suppressing private feuding for good.
Standardizing legal codes across previously fragmented jurisdictions — modern states impose one law where many had operated locally.
Centralizing taxation through professional bureaucracies — modern states extract from subjects in ways earlier sovereigns could not.
context: Society Must Be Defended (1976 lectures), History of Sexuality v.1. Biopolitics is one half of Foucault's late picture; discipline is the other.

question: Peirce gave a rule in 1878 for clearing up philosophical disputes. Ask, he said, what practical difference would follow if the idea were true. Two beliefs predicting exactly the same experience under every test are not really in dispute. What did he call the rule?
answer: The pragmatic maxim — the meaning of an idea is the sum of its conceivable practical consequences for action and experience.
choices: The pragmatic maxim — the meaning of an idea is the sum of its conceivable practical consequences for action and experience.
The principle of sufficient reason — every fact has an explanation, and any belief without one should be set aside until reasons appear.
The verification rule — a sentence is meaningful only if it can be empirically tested by observation under controlled experimental conditions.
The principle of charity — interpret an opponent's view as the strongest possible version, then test that version against your own commitments.
context: 'How to Make Our Ideas Clear' (1878). Peirce later renamed his view 'pragmaticism' to distance himself from what James did with it.

question: James in 'The Will to Believe' (1896) defended believing on incomplete evidence in a narrow class of cases. Critics — Russell sharpest — accused him of licensing wishful thinking. James's reply: the doctrine applies only when three conditions hold. A bet on Mars colonies fails. Why?
answer: The option is not 'forced' — you can suspend judgment and lose nothing, so the urgency that justifies belief without proof is absent.
choices: The option is not 'forced' — you can suspend judgment and lose nothing, so the urgency that justifies belief without proof is absent.
The hypothesis is too remote from ordinary experience — James restricted the doctrine to ideas drawn from everyday human social life.
The evidence is one-sided in favor of skepticism — James limited his rule to cases where the data weighed strongly toward the belief.
The hypothesis would not be testable in the believer's lifetime — James required practical verification before any belief was permitted.
context: Three conditions: the option must be living (a real possibility for you), forced (no easy abstention), and momentous (substantial stakes).

question: Dewey thought genuine inquiry begins only when habit fails — when something in your routine breaks and stops working. From there, the path runs through three steps before action resumes. What is the structure he proposed?
answer: A problematic situation interrupts habit; the mind frames hypotheses about what might fix it; the most promising is tested in practice, and revised as the world responds.
choices: A problematic situation interrupts habit; the mind frames hypotheses about what might fix it; the most promising is tested in practice, and revised as the world responds.
A problematic situation triggers a feeling; the feeling is examined through introspection; the inner verdict tells the agent what action ought to follow at that moment.
A problematic situation calls for authority; the agent consults the relevant expert; the expert pronounces, and the agent acts on the expert's conclusion in full.
A problematic situation reveals a deeper truth; the agent meditates until the truth becomes clear; the clarity itself is the resolution of the original puzzle.
context: How We Think (1910), Logic: The Theory of Inquiry (1938). Dewey treats inquiry as continuous with biological adaptation, not as a special philosophical activity.

question: Voltaire spent 1763 writing his Treatise on Tolerance after Jean Calas, a Protestant in Toulouse, was tortured to death on a false charge of murdering his son to stop a conversion. Voltaire's argument did not depend on showing one religion is true. What did he argue instead?
answer: No one knows enough about another person's salvation to harm them for their faith — religious doubt is the strongest case for letting people alone.
choices: No one knows enough about another person's salvation to harm them for their faith — religious doubt is the strongest case for letting people alone.
The Catholic Church had no historical right to its dominance in France — only state churches with older claims could legitimately suppress dissent.
The economic costs of persecution outweighed its supposed benefits — markets would punish intolerant cities by withdrawing trade and capital.
Religious truth would emerge naturally if persecutors simply waited — every false faith dies on its own within a few generations of its founding.
context: Treatise on Tolerance (1763). Voltaire's campaign eventually got the Calas verdict overturned posthumously — a consequential act of public advocacy.

question: Rousseau opens The Social Contract (1762) with one of the most famous lines in political philosophy: 'Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains.' Many take the line as complaint. Rousseau immediately complicates it. What does he ask in the very next sentences?
answer: Not how the chains arose, but how they can be made legitimate — what conditions would turn obedience into something rationally acceptable.
choices: Not how the chains arose, but how they can be made legitimate — what conditions would turn obedience into something rationally acceptable.
Whether the chains can be broken at all, and whether revolution is the only available means to do so given the strength of established regimes.
Who first placed the chains on humanity, and whether a specific historical event — the founding of agriculture — can be located as the moment.
How children should be educated to resist the chains, with the rest of the book treating political theory as an extension of pedagogy.
context: The Social Contract, Book I, ch. 1. Rousseau's general will is his answer: only laws each citizen could rationally will for all could legitimately bind.

question: Montesquieu in The Spirit of the Laws (1748) is remembered today as the source of 'separation of powers' — the doctrine America borrowed in 1787. The bigger argument of the book is less famous. Why, on his account, do the same laws work in one country and fail in another?
answer: Laws live inside a whole 'spirit' — climate, terrain, customs, religion, commerce — and any law that ignores its setting will not actually function there.
choices: Laws live inside a whole 'spirit' — climate, terrain, customs, religion, commerce — and any law that ignores its setting will not actually function there.
Some peoples are biologically suited to liberty and others to despotism, with national character being inherited rather than culturally formed by history.
Laws follow economic interest entirely; the underlying mode of production determines which legal arrangements will survive in any society.
Divine providence assigns each nation its government, and human reformers cannot alter what God has appointed for a particular people.
context: The Spirit of the Laws (1748). The argument is empirical and comparative — twenty years of work — and shaped Madison's Federalist 51.

question: Diderot spent twenty-five years editing the Encyclopédie — the great Enlightenment project to gather all reliable knowledge between two covers. Twenty-eight volumes, four thousand subscribers despite royal suppression. What was the editorial wager beneath the enterprise?
answer: If practical-arts and scientific knowledge were widely available, citizens could think for themselves and old authorities would weaken.
choices: If practical-arts and scientific knowledge were widely available, citizens could think for themselves and old authorities would weaken.
If learning could be made entertaining, popular literacy would rise sharply across France within two generations of the work's completion.
If a single comprehensive reference replaced scattered older books, the Catholic Church would lose its monopoly on the publishing trade.
If trade secrets were exposed publicly, French manufacturers could close the technological gap with their longer-established English rivals.
context: Encyclopédie, ou Dictionnaire raisonné des sciences, des arts et des métiers (1751–72). Diderot defended the project when partners abandoned him.

question: Francis Bacon in the Novum Organum (1620) listed four 'idols' that warp the human mind before evidence reaches it. Idols of the Tribe come from being human; Idols of the Cave from personal history. What was Bacon naming with the Idols of the Marketplace?
answer: Misleading effects of common language — vague words exchanged in conversation make muddled ideas look sharper than they really are.
choices: Misleading effects of common language — vague words exchanged in conversation make muddled ideas look sharper than they really are.
Distortions from political loyalty — what one's faction holds becomes harder to question, and group attachment overrides honest inquiry.
Greed and self-interest — the merchant's calculations bleed into intellectual life and bias the verdicts a free mind would reach unaided.
Sensory illusions — the eyes and ears mislead the mind in everyday perception in ways only careful instruments can finally correct.
context: Novum Organum, Book I. Bacon meant the marketplace literally — the spot where people exchange words as well as goods.

question: Newton's Principia (1687) gave a law of universal gravitation but offered no mechanism for how bodies pulled across empty space. Continental rivals — Leibniz especially — attacked this. Action at a distance, they said, was an occult quality dressed in mathematics. Newton's reply was terse. What did he say?
answer: 'Hypotheses non fingo' — I do not feign hypotheses. The mathematics describes the regularity; speculating about hidden mechanism is no part of his task.
choices: 'Hypotheses non fingo' — I do not feign hypotheses. The mathematics describes the regularity; speculating about hidden mechanism is no part of his task.
'Natura non facit saltus' — Nature does not make leaps. The continuity of motion ruled out any unbridgeable gap between distant gravitating bodies.
'Cogito ergo sum' — I think, therefore I am. The certainty of inner reflection alone justifies the conclusions arrived at in mathematical physics.
'Plus ultra' — further beyond. The unknown mechanism would be discovered by later generations, and current rejection of his law was simply premature.
context: General Scholium to the Principia, second edition (1713). Newton's stance shaped one strand of philosophy of science: describe; hold off on mechanism.

question: Galileo argued in The Assayer (1623) that some properties of objects — shape, number, motion — exist in the bodies themselves, while others — color, smell, taste — exist only as effects on the perceiver. The move was bedrock for the new physics. What did it let Galileo claim about mathematics?
answer: The 'book of nature' is written in mathematical characters — geometry handles the real properties; the rest is removed from natural science.
choices: The 'book of nature' is written in mathematical characters — geometry handles the real properties; the rest is removed from natural science.
Mathematics is a human convention with no special claim on physical reality, but a useful shorthand for what experimenters already know.
Natural philosophy must include theology, since the goal of inquiry is to understand the Creator's design lying behind the appearances.
Sense perception is wholly reliable for everyday life, and the philosopher's task is to systematize common sense rather than correct it.
context: The Assayer (1623). Locke later took up the distinction as primary/secondary qualities; Berkeley used it against material substance entirely.

question: Wittgenstein in the later Investigations asked a deceptively simple question: what do all games share? Chess, solitaire, ring-around-the-rosie, the Olympics. He listed candidate criteria — competition, rules, winning — and each failed for some game. What did he conclude?
answer: Words like 'game' do not name a shared essence — they pick out a 'family resemblance' of overlapping features with no single thread running through all.
choices: Words like 'game' do not name a shared essence — they pick out a 'family resemblance' of overlapping features with no single thread running through all.
Words like 'game' point to a Platonic Form in a separate realm, and the variety of cases shows how imperfectly any one game realizes its archetype.
Words like 'game' fail outright in any precise philosophical use, and ordinary speech should be replaced with stipulated technical vocabulary.
Words like 'game' name biological functions — playing has an evolutionary purpose, and every case shares whatever that purpose finally turns out to be.
context: Philosophical Investigations §§65–67. The image: features overlapping like resemblances in a family — eyes, nose, chin — with no feature shared by all.

question: Foucault opened the first volume of History of Sexuality (1976) by mocking what he called 'the repressive hypothesis' — the popular story that the Victorians silenced sex and the 20th century has been a long liberation since. He thought the story was historically backward. What did he find?
answer: Talk about sex exploded under the Victorians — medicine, law, religion, psychiatry generated endless classifications and confessions, not silence.
choices: Talk about sex exploded under the Victorians — medicine, law, religion, psychiatry generated endless classifications and confessions, not silence.
Sexual liberation has been an illusion — actual behavior has not changed much, and the language has only been adjusted to give the appearance of change.
Sex was discussed openly in 18th-century salons and then again from the 1960s, with the 19th century being a brief and atypical interruption.
Sexual mores follow climate and geography, not historical change — the Mediterranean has been steady for two thousand years while northern Europe has not.
context: History of Sexuality v.1 (1976). The opening reframed the field: not 'how was sex repressed?' but 'why have we built so many discourses around it?'

question: Hegel ended the Phenomenology of Spirit with 'absolute knowing' — Geist finally recognizing itself across the whole of its development. Critics from Schelling onward complained the picture had a strange feature. What did they object to?
answer: Hegel's system seemed to close history — once Geist has recognized itself, no genuinely new shape of spirit can appear, and human creativity is finished.
choices: Hegel's system seemed to close history — once Geist has recognized itself, no genuinely new shape of spirit can appear, and human creativity is finished.
Hegel's system reduced human persons to passive vehicles for Geist, with individual choice doing no real work in the unfolding of the dialectic.
Hegel's system depended on premises borrowed silently from theology, making it religious dogma dressed up in the costume of secular philosophy.
Hegel's system could not account for natural science, which had grown explosively since Kant and now ran on principles his dialectic could not capture.
context: The 'end of history' worry runs through Schelling, Kierkegaard, and Marx. Each took the diagnosis as a starting point for breaking with Hegel.

question: Marx in The German Ideology (1846, unpublished) advanced a thesis about the relationship between dominant ideas and dominant material conditions. The slogan version is famous. What does the slogan claim?
answer: The ruling ideas of any epoch are the ideas of its ruling class — those who own material production also control intellectual production.
choices: The ruling ideas of any epoch are the ideas of its ruling class — those who own material production also control intellectual production.
The ruling ideas of any epoch arise spontaneously from the people — folk culture remains underneath every elite ideology, waiting to surface again.
The ruling ideas of any epoch come from religious authority — control of dogma is what allows a class to hold power across the generations.
The ruling ideas of any epoch follow technology — each new productive technique forces a new worldview on rulers and workers together alike.
context: The German Ideology, 'Feuerbach.' The book was published posthumously in 1932. The thesis is the kernel of what later Marxists called the theory of ideology.

question: Simone de Beauvoir agreed with Sartre that freedom is the human condition. Yet in The Second Sex (1949) she argued a French woman in 1949 was not free in the way an Algerian colonial subject was not free. What did she say women experience that complicates the simple Sartrean picture?
answer: Women are made — through upbringing, custom, law, and language — into a 'second sex' whose freedom is constrained before any individual woman wakes up to it.
choices: Women are made — through upbringing, custom, law, and language — into a 'second sex' whose freedom is constrained before any individual woman wakes up to it.
Women are biologically determined by reproductive function — their lives must accommodate facts of childbearing that no political reform can eliminate entirely.
Women are entirely free in modern France — Beauvoir wrote to show that no further legal change was needed to bring women's freedom into being.
Women are oppressed only economically — Beauvoir argued the situation would resolve itself once industrial employment had become widely available to them.
context: The Second Sex (1949). Beauvoir's 'one is not born, but becomes, a woman' was a direct application of existentialist freedom to the situation she actually inhabited.

question: The Buddha taught that everything arises in dependence on conditions — no thing has its own self-standing being. He called this pratityasamutpada, dependent origination. Why does this not collapse into a chain of causes like physics?
answer: Each link conditions the next without producing it as cause produces effect — relations of mutual dependence, not one-way physical causation across time.
choices: Each link conditions the next without producing it as cause produces effect — relations of mutual dependence, not one-way physical causation across time.
Physical causation is one of the twelve links and is the same kind of process, but only the early portion of the Wheel is recognized by modern science.
Physical causation moves matter while dependent origination moves karma — two separate streams of events that never touch one another in any given life.
Physical causation is illusion at the conventional level; only mental events have real causal power and these alone constitute the twelve links of the chain.
context: The twelve nidanas describe how ignorance, formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the senses, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, becoming, birth, and aging-and-death condition one another. Buddhaghosa's Visuddhimagga distinguishes paccaya (condition) from hetu (cause) for exactly this reason — the relations are mutual and structural, not unidirectional event-by-event causation.

question: Nagarjuna taught two truths — conventional and ultimate. Critics charged he had simply built an exit door: speak emptiness when challenged, speak the world when convenient. How did he answer the charge?
answer: Without the conventional, the ultimate cannot be taught; without the ultimate, liberation cannot be reached — neither truth is a fallback, both are needed for the path itself.
choices: Without the conventional, the ultimate cannot be taught; without the ultimate, liberation cannot be reached — neither truth is a fallback, both are needed for the path itself.
Ultimate truth is the only truth and conventional speech is merely a teaching expedient with no philosophical standing of its own beyond practical convenience for monks.
Conventional truth is the only truth available to us and the ultimate is an aspirational ideal no living mind can grasp — Madhyamaka collapses into agnosticism here.
Both truths describe the same reality from different angles, the way two surveyors measure a mountain — what differs is the standpoint, not the world being measured.
context: Mulamadhyamakakarika 24.10. Nagarjuna's two-truths doctrine is structural, not optional. Conventional speech (samvrti-satya) is how the world functions; ultimate analysis (paramartha-satya) shows nothing has self-nature. Candrakirti and Tsongkhapa later disputed whether the conventional has any standing of its own — Tsongkhapa says yes, others say no — but Nagarjuna held both truths as load-bearing.

question: The Yogacara school argued that what we take for an outside world is structured by consciousness all the way down — vijnaptimatra, 'cognition-only.' Critics read this as Berkeleyan idealism. How does Vasubandhu's view differ?
answer: Berkeley's minds were stable individual substances that received ideas from God; Vasubandhu denied any standing substantial mind — only a stream of mental events conditioning further mental events.
choices: Berkeley's minds were stable individual substances that received ideas from God; Vasubandhu denied any standing substantial mind — only a stream of mental events conditioning further mental events.
Berkeley denied matter while keeping spirits real; Vasubandhu denied both matter and spirits, leaving only the formal patterns of Buddhist scripture as truly existing realities.
Berkeley argued ideas exist only when perceived by some mind; Vasubandhu argued ideas can exist unperceived in a storehouse, contradicting the very meaning of cognition-only.
Berkeley believed God grounds the regularity of experience; Vasubandhu replaced God with karma, but otherwise his metaphysics is the same Christian-style idealism in Buddhist clothing.
context: Vasubandhu's Vimsatika argued against external objects without thereby positing any abiding subject. The alaya-vijnana (storehouse consciousness) is itself a stream conditioned by karmic seeds — not a Cartesian or Berkeleyan substance. The comparison to Berkeley is one of the standard student errors that careful readers like Lusthaus and Garfield are at pains to correct.

question: The Buddha was asked by a disciple whether the world is eternal, whether the soul is the same as the body, what happens to a buddha after death — fourteen metaphysical questions in all. He refused to answer any of them. Why?
answer: A man shot with a poisoned arrow does not refuse treatment until he knows the archer's name — speculative questions delay the practical work of ending suffering.
choices: A man shot with a poisoned arrow does not refuse treatment until he knows the archer's name — speculative questions delay the practical work of ending suffering.
The questions presupposed metaphysical commitments that pious followers should accept on the Buddha's authority without troubling themselves about the underlying reasons.
The questions had been answered by earlier Vedic seers and the Buddha respected the Brahmanical settlement enough not to revisit ground already covered by older sages.
The questions concerned topics on which the Buddha simply lacked knowledge, since his enlightenment was about ethical conduct rather than cosmological matters of fact.
context: The Cula-Malunkyovada Sutta. The poisoned-arrow parable was the Buddha's reply: speculation about the cosmos is fine for those with leisure, but it does not pull the arrow out. The avyakata (undeclared) questions mark a methodological commitment — Buddhism is therapy first, metaphysics only insofar as it serves the therapy. The position contrasts sharply with Brahmanical philosophy of the same period.

question: Theravada Buddhists hold the arhat — one who has ended craving and will not be reborn — as the goal. Mahayana Buddhists reject this and hold the bodhisattva as higher. What is the bodhisattva's defining vow?
answer: To delay full nirvana until every sentient being has been carried across — liberation is not personal exit but universal commitment that takes lifetimes of work.
choices: To delay full nirvana until every sentient being has been carried across — liberation is not personal exit but universal commitment that takes lifetimes of work.
To master every sutra in the canon before claiming any spiritual attainment — knowledge of the texts is the precondition for any genuine release from the cycle of rebirth.
To remain in monastic discipline for at least one thousand lives — Theravada permits householders to attain arhatship, but Mahayana requires the monk's path for everyone.
To worship the buddhas of the ten directions through ritual offerings — bodhisattvas earn merit through devotion that arhats refuse to engage in out of austere pride.
context: The bodhisattva vow appears in many Mahayana texts including the Bodhicaryavatara of Santideva. The contrast with the Theravada arhat is doctrinal and structural — Mahayana texts often present arhats as having stopped short. The deeper philosophical point is that on Madhyamaka grounds (nothing has self-nature) a private liberation makes no sense; ones own freedom and others' are not finally separable.

question: Dignaga and Dharmakirti built a Buddhist epistemology around two and only two valid means of knowing — pratyaksa (perception) and anumana (inference). They rejected the Brahmanical sabda — scriptural testimony — as a third source. What was their reason?
answer: Testimony reduces to perception or inference once unpacked — either the speaker perceived something or inferred it, so the apparent third source dissolves under analysis.
choices: Testimony reduces to perception or inference once unpacked — either the speaker perceived something or inferred it, so the apparent third source dissolves under analysis.
Testimony presupposes a stable conventional language and Buddhism's doctrine of momentariness made any stable linguistic meaning a metaphysical impossibility to defend.
Testimony was reliable in the era of the Buddha but the gradual decline of dharma had so corrupted later teachers that the source could no longer be epistemically trusted.
Testimony as a source assumes a community of speakers stable enough to transmit it, and the doctrine of no-self made the existence of such a community internally incoherent.
context: Dignaga's Pramanasamuccaya and Dharmakirti's Pramanavarttika set out the two-pramana view that became the standard Buddhist epistemology in India and Tibet. The Brahmanical schools — especially Nyaya and Mimamsa — held testimony as an independent pramana, in Mimamsa's case to underwrite Vedic authority. The Buddhist reduction of testimony to perception-plus-inference is a careful logical move, not a dismissal of scripture.

question: Asanga's Yogacara school posited an alaya-vijnana, often translated 'storehouse consciousness' — a stream where karmic seeds wait to ripen. Critics from Madhyamaka charged that this had reinvented the self the Buddha had denied. How did Yogacara reply?
answer: The storehouse is itself a stream of momentary events with no abiding owner — what looks like a soul is just karmic continuity, no more substantial than a river named twice.
choices: The storehouse is itself a stream of momentary events with no abiding owner — what looks like a soul is just karmic continuity, no more substantial than a river named twice.
The storehouse is a real persisting substance and the Buddha's anatman doctrine was a teaching expedient appropriate only to listeners not yet ready for the deeper view.
The storehouse exists only at the conventional level and Madhyamaka critics had missed that Yogacara texts always meant the term as a metaphor for the body and brain.
The storehouse is identical with the dharmakaya (the buddha's body of truth) and so transcends the categories of self and not-self entirely from the start of the analysis.
context: Asanga's Mahayanasamgraha and Vasubandhu's Trimsika lay out the alaya-vijnana doctrine. Whether this constitutes a sneaky reintroduction of atman is a perennial Buddhist debate — Madhyamikas like Candrakirti pressed the charge; Yogacarins answered that the storehouse is a process, not a thing. Tibetan doxography preserved both readings as live positions.

question: Bodhidharma, the legend says, sat facing a cave wall for nine years in silence. When asked by Emperor Wu what merit he had earned by building monasteries, Bodhidharma replied, 'No merit.' What was he refusing?
answer: The transactional picture of merit — that good acts purchase a future reward — which he saw as itself the attachment keeping the emperor from awakening.
choices: The transactional picture of merit — that good acts purchase a future reward — which he saw as itself the attachment keeping the emperor from awakening.
The emperor's claim to authority over the sangha — Bodhidharma denied that any temporal ruler could meaningfully sponsor genuine practice from outside the monastery walls.
The use of vernacular Chinese for translating scripture — he insisted that the dharma could only be transmitted through Sanskrit until students had mastered the original language.
The traditional eight-fold path itself — Bodhidharma's school replaced it with sudden enlightenment alone, dispensing with right speech, right action, and the moral precepts.
context: The Bodhidharma–Wu exchange is preserved in the Blue Cliff Record. Bodhidharma's 'no merit' answer cuts the merit-economy at its root: aiming at reward is still self-seeking, even when the reward is enlightenment. The story is hagiography, but the philosophical point became central to Chan's distinctive flavor — practice not for gain, sitting that is already what it points toward.

question: Hakuin Ekaku revived Rinzai Zen in eighteenth-century Japan by systematizing koan study. He gave students an opening koan he had devised himself. What does 'the sound of one hand clapping' aim to do?
answer: Defeat the discursive mind's attempt to find a referent — there is no answer to fetch, and exhausting the search is where the practice begins.
choices: Defeat the discursive mind's attempt to find a referent — there is no answer to fetch, and exhausting the search is where the practice begins.
Test the student's familiarity with classical Chinese — the koan only makes sense in its original Tang-dynasty context, which Hakuin used as an entry exam for serious study.
Train the imagination to visualize impossible objects vividly — the meditative skill that Hakuin held was required for the more advanced visualizations later in the curriculum.
Convey the inseparability of action and inaction — the right hand cannot clap alone, just as conventional life cannot proceed without the support of monastic discipline.
context: Hakuin's 'sekishu no onjo' (the sound of one hand) was constructed to replace the older Mu koan as a fresh barrier for beginners. The point is not that there exists some hidden right answer that a clever student can deduce — koan practice in Rinzai uses such barriers to bring the discursive intellect to a halt, opening a different mode of seeing. The Soto school under Dogen emphasized shikantaza (just sitting) over koan work, marking a real intra-Zen split.

question: Dogen wrote that practice and enlightenment are not two — zazen is not a technique that produces awakening later, but is itself the awakening. What classical Buddhist picture was he rejecting?
answer: The means-end picture where meditation is a vehicle that delivers the practitioner to a separate destination called enlightenment somewhere down the road.
choices: The means-end picture where meditation is a vehicle that delivers the practitioner to a separate destination called enlightenment somewhere down the road.
The Pure Land picture where rebirth in Amida's paradise is the goal — Dogen held that paradise should be sought in this life rather than the next one as Pure Land taught.
The koan picture where intellectual breakthrough on a question is the milestone — Dogen rejected this in favor of devotional chanting drawn from earlier Tendai practice.
The bodhisattva picture where compassion for others is the orientation — Dogen redirected practitioners toward private self-cultivation in solitude apart from the wider community.
context: Dogen's Bendowa and the opening of Shobogenzo make the practice-realization (shusho-itto) point: zazen is not preparation for enlightenment, it is the activity of an already-buddha. This collapses the Mahayana picture inherited from India where bodhisattvas progress through stages. Soto Zen took this principle as central; Rinzai under Hakuin kept the koan-as-vehicle picture and the two schools have argued the point for eight centuries.

question: Zhiyi, founder of the Tiantai school in sixth-century China, taught the threefold truth — emptiness, provisionality, and the middle. He claimed this resolved a tension in Nagarjuna. What did he hold the middle truth was?
answer: The simultaneous holding of emptiness and provisionality at once — neither truth left behind in favor of the other, but each seen through the other in a single integrated view.
choices: The simultaneous holding of emptiness and provisionality at once — neither truth left behind in favor of the other, but each seen through the other in a single integrated view.
A compromise position somewhere between the extremes of emptiness and provisionality, calibrated case by case depending on which side of the doctrinal dispute appears stronger.
A higher third truth above the other two that absorbs them into itself — emptiness and provisionality are mere stepping-stones the advanced practitioner finally discards.
A pragmatic adjustment to the audience's level of understanding — the threefold truth is a pedagogical device with no ontological standing of its own beyond classroom utility.
context: Zhiyi's threefold truth (san-di) was an interpretation of Nagarjuna's Mulamadhyamakakarika 24.18 — 'emptiness, provisional designation, and the middle way.' Where Indian Madhyamaka generally took these as roughly synonymous, Zhiyi developed them as distinct but mutually entailing truths grasped together. The doctrine became foundational for the entire East Asian Buddhist synthesis, including Pure Land and Chan.

question: Confucius said the gentleman seeks harmony but not uniformity; the small person seeks uniformity but not harmony. He treated this as a deep difference between two ways of living together. What was the difference?
answer: Harmony tolerates real disagreement among parts that remain themselves; uniformity requires sameness and so destroys what would otherwise contribute to the whole.
choices: Harmony tolerates real disagreement among parts that remain themselves; uniformity requires sameness and so destroys what would otherwise contribute to the whole.
Harmony lets the wisest voice settle disputes once it has been identified by lengthy public examinations; uniformity rotates the privilege of leadership at fixed regular intervals.
Harmony emerges naturally from a population unified by shared blood and language; uniformity is the artificial product of a state that imposes one custom on diverse subjects.
Harmony is achieved when the lower classes obey the higher without question; uniformity requires the upper classes to lower themselves to manage the resentment of the governed.
context: Analects 13.23. The Chinese terms are he (harmony) and tong (sameness or agreement). The Analects often draws the distinction through cooking: a good broth blends sour and salt, bitter and sweet — each ingredient distinct, the dish a unified whole. A broth of only one taste is uniformity, not harmony. The Confucian gentleman aims at the broth.

question: Mencius told the story of a man who saw a child about to fall into a well and felt a sudden start of alarm — not from desire for the parents' favor, not from love of praise. From this case Mencius drew a sweeping claim about human nature. What was it?
answer: Human nature contains four innate sprouts of virtue including the heart of compassion — humans are good by nature and bad only when those sprouts are starved.
choices: Human nature contains four innate sprouts of virtue including the heart of compassion — humans are good by nature and bad only when those sprouts are starved.
Human action is governed by sympathy for kin and only extended sympathy by training reaches strangers — the child case is exceptional and most action follows the narrow pattern.
Human moral feeling is the product of social conditioning beginning in infancy — the alarm comes from early upbringing and cannot be relied on in the absence of careful teaching.
Human nature is a blank tablet on which any character can be written by ritual education — the alarm is evidence the man has been well taught, not of innate moral equipment.
context: Mencius 2A.6. The four sprouts (siduan) are compassion, shame, deference, and discernment of right and wrong — seeds of the four cardinal virtues. The child-and-the-well case is constructed to factor out all the reductionist explanations: the alarm precedes any thought of reward or reputation. Xunzi, Mencius's later opponent, ran the opposite argument from the same data.

question: Xunzi opposed Mencius and argued that human nature is bad. But he did not mean humans are evil in a moral sense the way some later readers heard him. What did he actually claim?
answer: Human nature is the bundle of raw desires we are born with — good must be made through ritual training, not awaited as something innate that already lies sleeping inside us.
choices: Human nature is the bundle of raw desires we are born with — good must be made through ritual training, not awaited as something innate that already lies sleeping inside us.
Human beings inherit guilt from earlier lives that ritual practice gradually wears down — until the karmic burden is cleared, the original goodness of the heart cannot emerge.
Human beings are radically corrupted by an original transgression from which only divine intervention can deliver them — Xunzi anticipated the later Christian doctrine here.
Human nature combines good and bad tendencies in equal measure and rests on the deliberate cultivation of one or the other through one's chosen company throughout life.
context: Xunzi's chapter Xing'e ('Human nature is bad'). His claim is closer to Hobbes than to Augustine: humans are not depraved, just unfinished. The raw nature must be transformed by li (ritual) and learning — and the master image is the carpenter who steams crooked wood straight, the potter who shapes clay. Mencius said the sprouts grow if watered; Xunzi said straightness must be imposed. The dispute defined classical Confucianism.

question: Zhu Xi, the neo-Confucian synthesizer of the twelfth century, taught that all things have two aspects — li (pattern, principle) and qi (vital energy, stuff). He used this to answer why people who share the same nature still differ morally. What was his answer?
answer: The pattern is the same in every person but the energy that carries it varies in clarity — some receive a clear qi that shows the pattern, others a turbid qi that obscures it.
choices: The pattern is the same in every person but the energy that carries it varies in clarity — some receive a clear qi that shows the pattern, others a turbid qi that obscures it.
The pattern itself differs across persons by birth and only its quantity is shared — some are simply allotted nobler patterns than others through the workings of cosmic justice.
The pattern is the same but encounters differ — each life supplies a unique sequence of situations and the variation among virtuous lives is entirely a matter of differing fortune.
The pattern and energy are equally varied across persons and the variation across moral lives reflects unique combinations of both without one dominating the other in importance.
context: Zhu Xi's li-qi metaphysics drew on the Yijing tradition and on Buddhist conceptual resources he largely opposed. The clear-qi/turbid-qi distinction lets him preserve Mencius's universal human nature while explaining apparent variation. Wang Yangming would later collapse this dualism, arguing that mind and pattern are one and that the work is not investigating things outside but extending innate knowing.

question: Wang Yangming broke with Zhu Xi on a famous case. Zhu had instructed him to investigate bamboo in his garden to discover its principle — Wang stared at it for a week, fell ill, and concluded the method was wrong. What did Wang come to teach instead?
answer: Liangzhi — the innate moral knowing already in the mind — needs only to be extended into action, not supplemented by outside investigation of patterns in distant objects.
choices: Liangzhi — the innate moral knowing already in the mind — needs only to be extended into action, not supplemented by outside investigation of patterns in distant objects.
The investigation of things in Zhu's sense should be replaced by chanting classical texts daily — knowing principle directly was beyond ordinary minds and required the scriptures.
Investigating outer things does work, but only for natural objects; the moral principles within human relationships required a separate empirical method drawn from the histories.
Both the inside-out and the outside-in routes are valid in their own spheres, and the sage uses each as the occasion demands without committing in advance to either pathway.
context: Wang Yangming's Chuanxilu records the bamboo episode and the doctrine of liangzhi (often rendered 'pure knowing' or 'innate moral knowledge'). The dispute with Zhu's school turns on whether moral cultivation is a project of outward investigation (Zhu) or inward extension (Wang). Both schools cited the Great Learning's 'investigation of things' as their key text — and read it in opposite directions. Wang's school dominated late Ming Confucianism.

question: Confucius placed ren — usually rendered humaneness or benevolence — at the center of his ethics. Yet when asked directly what ren is, he answered different students differently each time. What does this teaching pattern suggest about how he treated the virtue?
answer: Ren is not a definition to memorize but a way of responding to specific persons and situations — what counts as humane action varies with the particular case at hand.
choices: Ren is not a definition to memorize but a way of responding to specific persons and situations — what counts as humane action varies with the particular case at hand.
Ren has a single technical meaning but Confucius hid it deliberately from his lesser students, reserving the genuine teaching for an inner circle who would prove themselves worthy.
Ren is a vague placeholder that Confucius used to signal moral seriousness without committing to any concrete content — the variation reflects an absence of substantive theory.
Ren divides into ranked subtypes corresponding to social station, and Confucius assigned each student the version appropriate to the family rank into which they had been born.
context: Analects 6.30, 12.1, 12.2, 12.22, 13.19 and others all present ren differently — sometimes as restraining the self by ritual, sometimes as loving others, sometimes as a daily discipline. The variation is the teaching: ren is a virtue practiced in particulars, and what counts as humane treatment of a parent differs from humane treatment of a stranger. Aristotle's practical wisdom (phronesis) is structurally similar — and the comparison is genuinely illuminating.

question: Confucius held that the cultivated person treats parents with reverence at a higher pitch than the merely correct treatment of strangers. Critics from the rival Mohist school called this favoritism. What did Confucians answer?
answer: Graded love is realistic and trainable — moral concern that does not begin near home and extend outward is sentimental abstraction that cannot actually be lived out by humans.
choices: Graded love is realistic and trainable — moral concern that does not begin near home and extend outward is sentimental abstraction that cannot actually be lived out by humans.
Strangers are owed equal concern in principle but each station of life has its own preferred ritual practices that should not be applied indiscriminately across personal contexts.
Family preference is granted only as a transitional teaching for those not yet capable of impartial concern — the sage finally treats all persons identically in feeling and act.
Strangers and family are owed equal concern except in moments of crisis when family must come first; everyday morality treats them alike but emergencies sort out the priority.
context: Mozi's school argued for jian'ai (impartial concern), holding that biased love is the source of social conflict. Mencius (3B.9, 7A.45) replied that the Mohist position would have a person treat their own father like any stranger's father — and this, he said, is to be like a beast that has no father at all. The graded-love position became standard in Confucian ethics and resembles in structure the modern philosophical debate over agent-relative obligations.

question: Zhuangzi told of a cook butchering an ox for Lord Wenhui. The blade moved through joints and cavities without resistance, and the cook said his blade had been used nineteen years and was as sharp as the day it was forged. What philosophical lesson was Zhuangzi pressing?
answer: The skilled practitioner works with the natural grain rather than against it — effort is wasted on forcing matters and saved by following the patterns already there.
choices: The skilled practitioner works with the natural grain rather than against it — effort is wasted on forcing matters and saved by following the patterns already there.
Manual labor performed thoughtfully is morally superior to the abstract reasoning of philosophers — Zhuangzi praised the cook to embarrass intellectuals who do not work with their hands.
Mastery requires endless rehearsal of a fixed technique — the cook's blade lasts because he has repeated the same precise motions exactly the same way for nineteen straight years.
Even ugly tasks are dignified when performed for noble patrons — the lord's presence is what raises the butcher's craft to the level of philosophical example worth recording.
context: Zhuangzi, Chapter 3, 'The Secret of Caring for Life.' The cook is a paradigm of wu-wei — action that is so attuned to the situation that it appears effortless. The point is not laziness or quietism: the cook works hard, but works with the grain, finding the spaces where the blade can pass. Compare a modern surgeon who cuts along fascial planes rather than slicing across them. The story is one of Daoism's most cited because the lesson generalizes.

question: Zhuangzi told of a gnarled tree that lumberyards rejected — too crooked for beams, too knotted for boards. Local people called it useless. Zhuangzi answered that the tree had lived for a thousand years for exactly that reason. What was his philosophical claim?
answer: What a society calls useful destroys the thing called useful — survival often lies in being invisible to a system of value that consumes what it praises.
choices: What a society calls useful destroys the thing called useful — survival often lies in being invisible to a system of value that consumes what it praises.
What a society calls useful changes slowly over generations as needs shift and rejected items eventually find their place — patience is the deepest political and aesthetic virtue.
What a society calls useful tracks the deepest needs of its members reliably enough — the lumberyard is wise even when individual cases of waste occur on the margins of practice.
What a society calls useful is determined by its rulers and reflects their narrow interests — the people themselves usually recognize broader use that the elite ignores.
context: Zhuangzi, Chapter 4, 'In the World of Men.' The useless tree appears alongside the cripple Shu, the hunchback shaman, and other figures rejected by conventional standards. Zhuangzi's point cuts at both Confucian instrumentalism and Mohist utilitarianism: what counts as use depends on a frame, and the frame itself can be the source of harm. The useless flourishes where the useful is consumed.

question: Zhuangzi wrote that the fish trap exists for the fish; once you have the fish, you can forget the trap. Words exist for the meaning; once you have the meaning, you can forget the words. He concluded with a wish about other people. What did he wish for?
answer: A man who has forgotten words so that he might have a word with such a one — companion in seeing past the medium to what the medium had been for.
choices: A man who has forgotten words so that he might have a word with such a one — companion in seeing past the medium to what the medium had been for.
A man who had mastered words completely so that no nuance ever escaped him — the sage's ideal partner is the one who can be relied on never to misread a careful argument.
A man who refused to speak at all in any circumstance — silence is the only proper response of the wise once language has been seen through and finally set aside.
A man who spoke only the technical vocabulary of his trade — workers and craftsmen escape the snare of speculative talk that ruins the speech of philosophers and officials.
context: Zhuangzi, Chapter 26, 'External Things.' The fish-trap passage is one of the philosophical jokes that earns Zhuangzi his reputation: he undercuts even his own elaborate prose. Words point at what is wordless, and the wise reader passes through the saying to what it indicates, leaving the words behind. The Chan tradition would later treat this passage as a key text on language's relation to insight.

question: The Daodejing opens with one of philosophy's strangest sentences: 'The Dao that can be spoken is not the constant Dao; the name that can be named is not the constant name.' What argument is Laozi making about language?
answer: Naming carves a fluid reality into bounded items; the more precisely you name, the more you lose the unbroken whole the name was trying to point toward.
choices: Naming carves a fluid reality into bounded items; the more precisely you name, the more you lose the unbroken whole the name was trying to point toward.
Names are conventional and arbitrary signs and the wise person uses any naming system without believing in it — Laozi shares the Mohist functional view of language here.
Names refer to ideas in the speaker's mind rather than to anything in the world outside it — Laozi anticipated the British empiricists' representational theory by two thousand years.
Names work well for everyday objects but fail for sacred matters that only privileged ritual specialists are entitled to discuss in their proper hereditary technical vocabulary.
context: Daodejing, Chapter 1. The Chinese verb 'dao' is itself a near-pun: dao means both the Way and to speak. So the line literally reads: 'The way that can be wayed is not the constant way.' Speaking the way already departs from it, since speaking requires fixed concepts and the way is just what cannot be fixed. The point is not mysticism — it is a careful observation about what naming inherently does to its objects.

question: Laozi wrote that knowing others is intelligence, but knowing oneself is enlightenment. Conquering others requires force, but conquering oneself requires strength. Critics charged that this teaching is private and unpolitical. How does the Daodejing answer?
answer: Rulers who have not mastered themselves project unmastered impulses onto the realm — the deepest political work is the inner work that prevents bad rule from arising at all.
choices: Rulers who have not mastered themselves project unmastered impulses onto the realm — the deepest political work is the inner work that prevents bad rule from arising at all.
Inner cultivation is private preparation for genuine political action later, in the same way Aristotle's contemplative life sets up for full participation in the civic affairs of the polis.
Inner mastery is the prize of a quietist withdrawal from politics — Laozi advised the sage to abandon the dusty world entirely and tend only the garden of the inner heart.
Inner conquest replaces outer rule altogether — Laozi taught a kind of philosophical anarchism in which any form of organized government is to be dismantled by collective effort.
context: Daodejing, Chapter 33. Laozi addresses the Daodejing partly to the ruler (it is sometimes called a manual for kings). The inner-outer claim is not quietist: an unmastered ruler unleashes appetites that produce wars, levies, and famines. Mastery of self is therefore the precondition for the wu-wei ruler whose people, looking back, say 'we did this ourselves.' The argument is structurally close to Marcus Aurelius — and to Burke on the inseparability of self-government from self-restraint.

question: Zhuangzi argued that what we call right and wrong, this and that, beautiful and ugly are all generated from a perspective. A frog in a well thinks the sky is small. From this he drew a striking philosophical conclusion. What was it?
answer: No standpoint outside all perspectives exists from which to settle the disputes — what looks like the world from one frame and another are equally real frames of a shared reality.
choices: No standpoint outside all perspectives exists from which to settle the disputes — what looks like the world from one frame and another are equally real frames of a shared reality.
Every perspective is an illusion that the sage dispels by direct unmediated perception of the Dao — the well-frog and the philosopher share a common error that wisdom removes.
One privileged perspective — the sage's view from the mountain — is veridical and the others are not — Zhuangzi defends an esoteric realism beneath the perspectivist surface play.
Each perspective contains its own internal truth that conflicts with no other and the perspectives can be added together arithmetically into a single coherent universal account.
context: Zhuangzi, Chapter 2, 'Discussion on Making All Things Equal.' Zhuangzi's perspectivism is sometimes called proto-relativism, but it is more nuanced than that label suggests — he holds that perspectives are real and useful, not that all judgments are equally good. The point is that an absolute external standpoint is a fantasy. Nietzsche later made a structurally similar argument, and the parallel is genuinely illuminating without flattening either thinker.

question: Daoism shares with Confucianism the term de — usually rendered 'virtue' or 'power.' But Daoist de means something different from Confucian de. What is the contrast that the Daodejing presses?
answer: Confucian de is cultivated character that earns moral standing; Daoist de is the inherent power a thing has when it is fully itself, without effort to be anything other than what it is.
choices: Confucian de is cultivated character that earns moral standing; Daoist de is the inherent power a thing has when it is fully itself, without effort to be anything other than what it is.
Confucian de belongs to humans only and to humans only after deliberate training; Daoist de is the property of any natural object whatsoever and lacks any specifically moral content at all.
Confucian de is taught through ritual practice in the village school; Daoist de is acquired through ascetic discipline practiced in the mountains far from the corrupting influence of cities.
Confucian de is a public reputation built across many years; Daoist de is the inner felt sense of one's own goodness that requires no outside witness or acknowledgement in any form.
context: Daodejing chapters 38, 51, and 65 develop Daoist de. The line in chapter 38 — 'The highest de is not de, and so it has de; the lowest de does not lose de, and so it has no de' — pokes directly at the Confucian project of self-conscious cultivation. Daoist de is more like what a sharp knife or a clear stream has: it is the way that thing works when nothing obstructs its functioning. Confucian de is a moral inheritance accumulated through effort; the two readings of the same word run on different rails.

question: Ramanuja accepted Sankara's claim that Brahman is one but rejected the further claim that the world's plurality is illusion. He called his view visistadvaita — qualified non-dualism. What did the qualification do?
answer: It made the world and individual souls real but dependent — distinct features of Brahman, not separate from it, in the way a body and its parts are one substance with real differences.
choices: It made the world and individual souls real but dependent — distinct features of Brahman, not separate from it, in the way a body and its parts are one substance with real differences.
It introduced a second eternal principle alongside Brahman to account for matter — a dualism similar to Samkhya's purusa and prakriti, recovering plurality at a fundamental level.
It split Brahman into two persons — one personal and worshipped, one impersonal and beyond worship — through which devotees access the divine according to their temperament.
It rejected the authority of the Upanishads in favor of the Bhagavad Gita alone — Ramanuja held that the Gita's bhakti theology should override the older non-dualist texts entirely.
context: Ramanuja (c. 1017-1137) wrote the Sribhasya on the Brahma Sutras to argue that Sankara's Advaita (radical non-dualism) made bhakti — devotion — incoherent: you cannot love what is identical with you. Visistadvaita preserves the dependence of soul and world on Brahman without collapsing them into Brahman. The body-soul analogy lets the world be real and Brahman remain one. Later Madhva would push further to Dvaita (full dualism), making three live positions in Vedanta.

question: Nyaya, the school of logic and epistemology, defended four valid means of knowing where Buddhists allowed only two. The fourth — sabda — is verbal testimony. Why did Nyaya defend testimony so vigorously?
answer: Reliable testimony from a competent speaker carries information neither perception nor inference can supply — denying it leaves most of what any human actually knows without epistemic standing.
choices: Reliable testimony from a competent speaker carries information neither perception nor inference can supply — denying it leaves most of what any human actually knows without epistemic standing.
Testimony was the only valid source for the Vedas and rejecting it would have left the Vedas without epistemic backing — the rest of the defense is just window-dressing on this religious motive.
Testimony was needed to refute Buddhist arguments since Buddhist scriptures are themselves transmitted by testimony — Nyaya wanted to expose what it saw as Buddhist internal inconsistency.
Testimony was practical and useful even if not strictly valid — Nyaya allowed it on pragmatic grounds for ordinary discourse but never as a basis for genuine philosophical demonstration.
context: Nyayasutra 1.1.7 defines sabda as 'the assertion of a reliable person.' The school's defense is structural, not religious — though its application to the Vedas was clearly part of the motivation. Gangesa later refined the account in his Tattvacintamani. The contrast with Buddhist Dignaga, who reduced testimony to inference, is one of the most carefully argued debates in classical Indian philosophy, with each side meeting the other's strongest objections.

question: Mimamsa, the oldest of the six orthodox schools, faced a problem about the eternity of the Vedas. The Vedas had to be eternal to ground their authority but words seem to arise and pass away when spoken. What was the school's solution?
